|access-date=2 July 2024 |df=dmy }}</ref> |mp = [[Richard Tice]] |party = [[Reform UK]] |region = England |county = [[Lincolnshire]] |towns = [[Boston, Lincolnshire|Boston]], [[Hubberts Bridge]], [[Skegness]], [[Swineshead, Lincolnshire|Swineshead]], [[Wainfleet, Lincolnshire|Wainfleet]] |national = |westminster = |european = East Midlands }} '''Boston and Skegness''' is a [[United Kingdom constituencies#County constituencies and borough constituencies|county constituency]], represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[UK Parliament]]. It is located in [[Lincolnshire]], England. Like all British constituencies, Boston and Skegness elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first-past-the-post]] system of election. The seat has been represented by the Reform UK MP, Richard Tice since the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 General Election]] and was usually considered a [[safe seat]] for the Conservatives.
The constituency was created in 1997, from parts of the former constituencies of [[Holland with Boston]] and [[East Lindsey (UK Parliament constituency)|East Lindsey]]. The constituency has always elected a Conservative MP. In the [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997]] and [[2001 United Kingdom general election|2001]] general elections, the seat was very [[marginal seat|marginal]], with majorities of less than 1,000 votes for the Conservative candidate over the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] candidate. The next two general elections, in [[2005 United Kingdom general election|2005]] and [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010]], saw large [[Swing (politics)|swings]] towards the Conservatives. In the 2015 general election, the [[Eurosceptic]] [[UK Independence Party]] (UKIP) overtook Labour to take second place in the constituency; the party won 33.8% of the vote in the seat, which was UKIP's second-highest vote share in any constituency in that election (after [[Clacton (UK Parliament constituency)|Clacton]]). The seat had been one of UKIP's top target seats in that election, as they had also performed strongly in the constituency at the two previous general elections.
The constituency is estimated to have had the highest vote share in favour of leaving the [[European Union]] (EU) in the [[2016 EU membership referendum]], at 75.6%. For this reason, the leader of UKIP, [[Paul Nuttall]], stood as the party's candidate in the seat in the [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017 general election]]. UKIP's vote share fell nationally that election, and they dropped to third place (behind Labour) with 7.7% of the vote, the party's third largest percentage drop in vote share. In the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019 general election]], the Conservatives increased their majority further, winning 76.7% of the vote. This was their second-highest vote share in the election (after [[Castle Point (UK Parliament constituency)|Castle Point]]). The seat was also the second-safest Conservative seat in that election (measured by swing needed for the second-place party to gain the seat), after the neighbouring seat of [[South Holland and the Deepings]].
==Boundaries==
=== Historic === In England, constituency boundaries are determined by the [[Boundary Commission for England]], an independent body which periodically reviews the size of each constituency based on demographic data; these changes must be approved by the [[UK Parliament]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-37337175 |title=Boundary changes: Why UK's political map is being re-drawn |last=Stamp |first=Gavin |date=13 September 2016 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201134110/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-37337175 |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020 |quote=The shake-up - drawn up by the independent Boundary [Commission] of England}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.parliament.uk/about/how/elections-and-voting/constituencies/ |title=Parliamentary constituencies |author=<!--Not stated--> |publisher=UK Parliament |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202095932/https://www.parliament.uk/about/how/elections-and-voting/constituencies/ |url-status=live |archive-date=2 February 2020 |access-date=2 February 2020 |quote=Both Houses of Parliament need to agree any changes}}</ref> The constituency of Boston and Skegness was created as a [[United Kingdom constituencies#County constituencies and borough constituencies|county constituency]],{{efn|Constituencies in the United Kingdom are legally designated as either ''county constituencies'' or ''borough constituencies''.{{sfn|Boundary Commission for England|2018|p=5}} In general, county constituencies are any constituencies where more than a small proportion of the constituency is rural.{{sfn|Boundary Commission for England|2018|p=6}} Legally, campaign spending limits are higher in county constituencies than in borough constituencies,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-30477250 |title=2015 election campaign officially begins on Friday |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=18 December 2014 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201140106/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-30477250 |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020 |quote=9p per voter in county constituencies, and 6p per voter in borough seats}}</ref> and the two categories of seats have different types of [[Returning officer#United Kingdom|returning officers]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.electoralcommission.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-11/UKPGE-LGE%20Part%20A%20-%20Returning%20Officer%20role%20and%20responsibilities.pdf |title=Part A – (Acting) Returning Officer role and responsibilities |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=November 2019 |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (United Kingdom)|Electoral Commission]] |page=8 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208223553/https://www.electoralcommission.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-11/UKPGE-LGE%20Part%20A%20-%20Returning%20Officer%20role%20and%20responsibilities.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020 |quote=In a borough constituency contained in a district, the mayor or chairman of the local authority is the RO [returning officer]. In a county constituency, the RO is the Sheriff of the County}}</ref> }} by a [[Statutory instrument (UK)|statutory instrument]] in 1994, as part of the [[Fourth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], and was first contested in the [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997 general election]]. When formed, it consisted of the [[Borough of Boston]] and the [[Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom|wards]] of Burgh le Marsh, Friskney, Frithville, Ingoldmells, St Clement's, Scarbrough, Seacroft, Sibsey, Wainfleet, and Winthorpe in the [[East Lindsey|District of East Lindsey]].<ref>{{Cite legislation UK |type=si |year=1995 |number=1626 |si=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1995}}</ref> The constituency was largely created from parts of the former [[Holland with Boston (UK Parliament constituency)|Holland with Boston constituency]], with the remainder previously part of the former seat of [[East Lindsey (UK Parliament constituency)|East Lindsey]].{{sfn|Waller|Criddle|1999|p=90}}
The constituency boundaries changed at the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]] as part of the [[Fifth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], bringing in the two wards of Stickney and Croft from the neighbouring constituency of [[Louth and Horncastle]].<ref name=2007boundaries/> The constituency then consisted of the Borough of Boston, and the District of East Lindsey wards of Burgh le Marsh, Croft, Frithville, Ingoldmells, St Clement's, Scarbrough, Seacroft, Sibsey, Stickney, Wainfleet and Friskney, and Winthorpe.<ref name=2007boundaries>{{Cite legislation UK |type=si |year=2007 |number=1681 |si=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007}}</ref> The original proposal from the Boundary Commission had been to only transfer the Croft ward, but it was then decided to also include the ward of Stickney because of its ties with the town of [[Boston, Lincolnshire|Boston]].{{sfn|Boundary Commission for England|2007|pp=372, 375}}
The [[Sixth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]] was carried out between 2011 and 2018. The review recommended that two wards – Heckington Rural, and Kirkby la Thorpe and South Kyme – be transferred to Boston and Skegness from the constituency of [[Sleaford and North Hykeham]];{{sfn|Boundary Commission for England|2018|pp=44–45}} however the review was not implemented and its results were formally laid aside in 2020.
Boston and Skegness is bordered by the constituencies of Louth and Horncastle to the north, Sleaford and North Hykeham to the west, and [[South Holland and The Deepings]] to the south; all three of these constituencies are in the county of [[Lincolnshire]] and are all considered safe Conservative seats,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/politics/constituencies/E14000714 |title=What are the issues for Lincolnshire voters? |last=Edwards |first=Sharon |date=13 December 2019 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208185245/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/politics/constituencies/E14000714 |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020 |quote=Lincolnshire is a true blue stomping ground with six of the seven seats taken by Conservative candidates in 2017 and none with a majority of less than 16,000.}}</ref> and have been represented by MPs from the party since the formation of the constituencies in 1997. Indeed, as of the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019 general election]], all seven [[List of Parliamentary constituencies in Lincolnshire|Parliamentary constituencies in Lincolnshire]] have a Conservative MP.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election-2019-50774478 |title=General election 2019: Tories retake Lincoln |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=13 December 2019 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200203170417/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election-2019-50774478 |url-status=live |archive-date=3 February 2020 |access-date=3 February 2020 |quote=The party now controls all seven of Lincolnshire's parliamentary constituencies}}</ref>
=== Current boundaries === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which comes into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 December 2020):
* The Borough of Boston. * The District of East Lindsey wards of Burgh le Marsh; Chapel St. Leonards; Croft; Friskney; Ingoldmells; St. Clement's; Scarbrough & Seacroft; Sibsey & Stickney; Wainfleet; Willoughby with Sloothby; Winthorpe.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part I}}</ref>
''The constituency was expanded to include the two East Lindsey District wards of Chapel St Leonards and Willoughby with Sloothby, transferred from [[Louth and Horncastle]].''
==Constituency profile== [[File:BostonStump.JPG|thumb|upright=1.5|alt=A small river, with houses on either side and a church spire in the background|[[Boston, Lincolnshire|Boston]], with the spire of [[St Botolph's Church, Boston|St Botolph’s Church]] (the ‘Boston Stump’) in the background]] [[File:Clock Tower, Skegness 1.JPG|thumb|upright=1.5|alt=A fountain with a sculpture of a person; a clock tower, people and buildings are in the background|The centre of [[Skegness]] with its clock-tower ]]
{{Blockquote |text=The market town of Boston is an important administrative centre for rural Lincolnshire, and its modernised port, which brings thousands of tonnes of steel, timber and paper into the constituency, a key employer. Light industry and food processing are the other major industries in the town and surrounding villages, but elsewhere agriculture remains dominant. The resort of Skegness has recovered from a damaging dip in trade caused by pit closures in the East Midlands during the 1980s, and following regeneration through millions of pounds in EU grants, is now one of Britain’s most popular resorts, particularly among the elderly during the winter months. |source=[[BBC News]], 2001<ref name=bbc2001/>}}
Boston, Lincolnshire, is a historic town,<ref name="disctowns">{{cite web |title=The historic town of Boston in Lincolnshire |url=https://www.discoverbritainstowns.co.uk/uncategorised/boston/ |website=Discover Britain’s Towns |access-date=6 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200506142540/https://www.discoverbritainstowns.co.uk/uncategorised/boston/ |archive-date=6 May 2020 |date=2 September 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> famous for the tower of [[St Botolph's Church, Boston|St Botolph's Church]], known by locals as the "Stump".<ref name=bostonchanged>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-eu-referendum-36258541 |title=How immigration changed Boston, Lincolnshire |last=Cook |first=Chris |date=10 May 2016 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202164745/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-eu-referendum-36258541 |url-status=live |archive-date=2 February 2020 |access-date=2 February 2020}}</ref> [[Skegness]] is a seaside town and holiday destination; the first [[Butlins]] resort opened in Skegness in 1936.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/uk/80-years-of-british-family-holidays-at-butlins-a6971046.html |title=80 years of British family holidays at Butlin's |last=Calder |first=Simon |date=7 April 2016 |work=The Independent |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202165818/https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/uk/80-years-of-british-family-holidays-at-butlins-a6971046.html |url-status=live |archive-date=2 February 2020 |access-date=2 February 2020}}</ref>
The constituency has a lower level of qualifications (measured by [[National Vocational Qualification]]s) than the East Midlands average and the average for Great Britain;<ref name=profile>{{cite web |url=http://www.nomisweb.co.uk/reports/lmp/wpca/1929379893/report.aspx |title=Labour Market Profile - Boston And Skegness Parliamentary Constituency |website=Nomis |publisher=[[Office for National Statistics]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200119140142/http://www.nomisweb.co.uk/reports/lmp/wpca/1929379893/report.aspx |url-status=live |archive-date=19 January 2020 |access-date=19 January 2020}}</ref> in 2018, 19.7% of the adult population had a [[Higher National Diploma]] or degree-level qualification, compared to the British average of 39.3%.<ref name=profile/> The 2015 data also found that the median house price in the constituency was £125 000.<ref name=visualising>{{cite web |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/articles/visualisingyourconstituency/2015-03-26 |title=Visualising your constituency |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=26 March 2015 |publisher=Office for National Statistics |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202162644/https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/articles/visualisingyourconstituency/2015-03-26 |url-status=live |archive-date=2 February 2020 |access-date=2 February 2020}}</ref> In 2019, the average gross weekly pay for people working full-time was £462, lower the average for Great Britain, which was £587.<ref name=profile/> The most common jobs are process plant and machine operatives and sales and customer service occupations. Around 40% of workers work in one of these areas, more than twice the national average.<ref name=profile/> The constituency also has a lower employment rate and a higher level of people on unemployment benefits than the averages for the region and the country.<ref name=profile/>
According to the [[2011 UK Census]], Boston was "home to a higher proportion of Eastern European immigrants than anywhere else in England and Wales".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/dec/11/census-boston-eastern-european-immigration |title=Census reveals rural town of Boston has most eastern European immigrants |last=Pidd |first=Helen |date=11 December 2012 |work=[[The Guardian]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200130134800/https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/dec/11/census-boston-eastern-european-immigration |url-status=live |archive-date=30 January 2020 |access-date=30 January 2020}}</ref> People born in other EU countries, most of whom came from Eastern Europe after the [[2004 enlargement of the European Union]], made up 13% of the town's population.<ref name=bostonchanged/> The BBC described the town as "one of the most extreme examples in Britain of a town affected by recent EU immigration".<ref name=bostonchanged/> In 2015, 11.3% of people living in the constituency were born outside the UK.<ref name=visualising/> The average age in the constituency was 32 at the time.<ref name=visualising/>
==History== {{very long section|date=January 2024}} Like all [[UK Parliament constituencies]], Boston and Skegness elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) using the [[first-past-the-post]] [[voting system]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-50249649 |title=General election 2019: What is the secret behind tactical voting? |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=13 November 2019 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200203081244/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-50249649 |url-status=live |archive-date=3 February 2020 |access-date=3 February 2020 |quote=The UK uses a first-past-the-post voting system, sometimes described as "winner takes all"}}</ref>
===1997–2001: Marginal seat between Conservatives and Labour=== The constituency was created in 1997 from parts of the former constituencies of [[Holland with Boston]] and [[East Lindsey (UK Parliament constituency)|East Lindsey]]. The in part predecessor area's veteran MP [[Richard Body]], who had been MP for Holland with Boston between 1966 and 1997, held the seat at the 1997 general election with a 1.4% majority (647 votes).{{sfn|Morgan|2001a|p=80}} The seat had been formed from two constituencies held by the Conservatives with large majorities, and a Conservative victory was seen as very likely. However, the election result nationally was a landslide victory for the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]], and Body only narrowly remained in Parliament; the seat was the tenth most marginal Conservative-held seat at the election by percentage majority and the ninth most marginal by absolute majority (number of votes).{{sfn|Morgan|2001a|p=80}}{{sfn|Waller|Criddle|1999|p=lv}} The academics [[Robert Waller (pundit)|Robert Waller]] and [[Byron Criddle]] attributed his victory to the [[Referendum Party|Referendum Party's]] decision not to stand, which they did because of Body's [[Euroscepticism in the United Kingdom|Eurosceptic]] views.{{sfn|Waller|Criddle|1999|p=90}}
After retiring from Parliament, Body left the Conservatives and joined the [[UK Independence Party]] (UKIP), a party that supported British withdrawal from the European Union (EU), though he encouraged people to vote Conservative at the [[2005 United Kingdom general election|2005 general election]].<ref name=bodyretires>{{cite web |url=http://www.totalpolitics.com/history/149237/where-are-they-now-sir-richard-body.thtml |title=Where are they now? Sir Richard Body |date=4 March 2011 |work=[[Total Politics]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130405045750/http://www.totalpolitics.com/history/149237/where-are-they-now-sir-richard-body.thtml |url-status=dead |archive-date=5 April 2013 |access-date=2 February 2020}}</ref> His membership later lapsed and he defected to the [[English Democrats]], a small [[far-right]] party.<ref name=bodyretires/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2014/05/whatever-happened-english-democrats |title=Whatever happened to the English Democrats? |last=Trilling |first=Daniel |date=15 May 2014 |work=[[New Statesman]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202102814/https://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2014/05/whatever-happened-english-democrats |url-status=live |archive-date=2 February 2020 |access-date=2 February 2020 |quote=Peter Davis's election as mayor of Doncaster remains the far-right fringe party's biggest achievement}}</ref>
Body's successor, the Conservative [[Mark Simmonds]], won an even smaller majority of 1.3% over Labour in the [[2001 United Kingdom general election|2001 general election]] (515 votes). The seat was described by Waller and Criddle as "an exceptionally tight two-way marginal".{{sfn|Waller|Criddle|2002|p=158}} The seat was the fourth most marginal Conservative seat at that election (by both percentage and absolute majority) and the most marginal Conservative seat with Labour in second place.{{sfn|Morgan|2001b|pp=28–29}}{{sfn|Waller|Criddle|2002|p=35}}
===2001–2010: Labour support falls, UKIP perform strongly=== In the 2005 general election, Simmonds increased his majority over Labour to 14.1%. The seat had the 139th largest absolute majority and the 131st largest percentage majority out of the 198 Conservative seats.{{sfn|Mellows-Facer|2006|pp=128–130}} Richard Horsnell, the candidate for the anti-European Union party [[UKIP]] (United Kingdom Independence Party) came third with 9.6%. This was UKIP's highest vote share in any seat in the 2005 general election, with the exception of [[South Staffordshire (UK Parliament constituency)|South Staffordshire]], where UKIP won 10.4% after the election was delayed due to the death of a candidate.{{sfn|Mellows-Facer|2006|pp=22, 47, 123, 152}}<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk_politics/4098284.stmwe |title=The longest campaign |last=Wheeler |first=Brian |date=17 June 2005 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131155443/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/4098284.stm |url-status=live |archive-date=31 January 2020 |access-date=31 January 2020 |quote=this tragic event meant the general election would have to be postponed in Staffordshire South}}</ref> UKIP also performed strongly in several local council elections in Boston on the same day, winning more than 20% of the vote in some wards.{{sfn|Waller|Criddle|2007|p=200}} Overall, UKIP won 2.2% of the national vote and won an average of 2.8% in the seats they stood candidates in.{{sfn|Mellows-Facer|2006|p=47}} Meanwhile, the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]] fell from third to fourth place with just 8.7% of the vote; this was the party's seventh-lowest vote share in any seat, and third-lowest vote share in a constituency in England, in the election.{{sfn|Mellows-Facer|2006|p=125}} Waller and Criddle said that the constituency "now looks like a fairly safe Tory [Conservative] seat", though Labour had hoped to win the seat in the election.{{sfn|Waller|Criddle|2007|pp=199–200}}
After his re-election, Simmonds was appointed Shadow Minister for International Development in May 2005, before being moved to be a Shadow Health Minister in July 2007.<ref name=rthon>{{cite web |url=https://members.parliament.uk/member/1393/career |title=Rt Hon Mark Simmonds |author=<!--Not stated--> |year=2015 |publisher=[[UK Parliament]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201172508/https://members.parliament.uk/member/1393/career |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020 |quote=Shadow Minister (Health) Department of Health 3 July 2007 - 6 May 2010}}</ref>
In the 2010 general election, Simmonds increased his majority over Labour further, winning almost half the vote compared to Labour's 20.6%. The Liberal Democrats came third, while UKIP achieved fourth place; their candidate Christopher Pain won 9.5% of the vote. This share of the vote was similar to the result in the previous election, and was UKIP's second-highest in 2010, after the special case of [[Buckingham (UK Parliament constituency)|Buckingham]].{{sfn|Rhodes|Cracknell|McGuiness|2011|p=94}}{{efn|Buckingham was at the time the seat of the [[Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)|Speaker of the House of Commons]], [[John Bercow]]; the Speaker is seen as neutral and is traditionally not challenged by major parties.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election-2019-50320790 |title=General election 2019: The town that won't get a choice |last1=Wright |first1=Katie |last2=Willis |first2=Ella |date=10 November 2019 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131134051/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election-2019-50320790 |url-status=live |archive-date=31 January 2020 |access-date=31 January 2020 |quote=tradition means major parties agree not to stand against the Speaker, who is considered to be politically neutral}}</ref> The Conservatives, Labour and the Liberal Democrats did not stand in the seat in the 2010 general election, but several minor party and independent candidates, including Farage, contested the seat and the race was seen as unusually competitive.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.economist.com/britain/2010/03/25/a-well-mannered-revolution |title=A well-mannered revolution? |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=25 March 2010 |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131134033/https://www.economist.com/britain/2010/03/25/a-well-mannered-revolution |url-status=live |archive-date=31 January 2020 |access-date=31 January 2020 |quote=Bercow also faces a serious challenge from UKIP's Mr Farage}}</ref> Farage came third, behind Bercow and an independent candidate, [[John Stevens (English politician)|John Stevens]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/shared/election2010/results/constituency/a79.stm |title=UK: England: South East: Buckingham |author=<!--Not stated--> |year=2010 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201172958/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/shared/election2010/results/constituency/a79.stm |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020}}</ref> }} The far-right<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2018/may/02/bnps-last-district-councillor-bows-out-but-insists-party-will-rise-again |title=As the BNP vanishes, do the forces that built it remain? |last=Pidd |first=Helen |date=2 May 2018 |work=The Guardian |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208184336/https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2018/may/02/bnps-last-district-councillor-bows-out-but-insists-party-will-rise-again |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020 |quote=With the far-right party’s last councillor retiring in Lancashire, its fall from grace is complete}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-47974579 |title=Facebook bans UK far right groups and leaders |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=18 April 2019 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208184733/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-47974579 |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020 |quote=Facebook has imposed a ban on a dozen far-right individuals and organisations that it says "spread hate". The ban includes the British National Party}}</ref> [[British National Party]] (BNP) also performed strongly in the constituency, winning 5.3% of the vote; since this was more than 5%, the party saved their [[Election deposit#United Kingdom|deposit]].{{sfn|Rhodes|Cracknell|McGuiness|2011|pp=94, 96}}
===2010–2015: Conservatives challenged by UKIP=== Following the 2010 general election, Simmonds became [[Parliamentary Private Secretary]] to [[Caroline Spelman]], the [[Secretary of State for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/defra-role-for-boston-mp-mark-simmonds-1-1117143 |work=[[Boston Standard]] |title=Defra role for Boston MP Mark Simmonds |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=29 June 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812204139/https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/defra-role-for-boston-mp-mark-simmonds-1-1117143 |archive-date=12 August 2014 |access-date=13 May 2013}}</ref> Following the [[2012 British cabinet reshuffle|2012 cabinet reshuffle]], he became the [[Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs]] a junior role in the [[Foreign and Commonwealth Office]].<ref name=rthon/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/update-foreign-office-reveals-boston-mp-s-responsibilities-after-reshuffle-appointment-1-4225660 |work=The Boston Standard |title=Update: Foreign Office reveals Boston MP's responsibilities after reshuffle appointment |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=6 September 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120915055357/https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/update-foreign-office-reveals-boston-mp-s-responsibilities-after-reshuffle-appointment-1-4225660 |archive-date=15 September 2012 |access-date=13 May 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fco.gov.uk/en/about-us/who-we-are/our-ministers/ |title=Our Ministers |author=<!--Not stated--> |year=2012 |publisher=Foreign and Commonwealth Office |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120906210937/http://www.fco.gov.uk/en/about-us/who-we-are/our-ministers/ |archive-date=6 September 2012 |access-date=7 February 2020}}</ref>
The polling company [[Survation]] analysed the results of the [[2013 United Kingdom local elections|2013 local elections]] and estimated that if UKIP were to perform equally well in a general election, then they would gain the constituency with an 11% majority. Of the ten constituencies that Survation predicted UKIP would win, Boston and Skegness had the largest predicted UKIP majority.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.survation.com/2013/05/ukip-won-in-8-westminster-constituencies-last-thursday/ |title=Local Election Analysis: UKIP "won" in 10 Westminster Constituencies |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=12 May 2013 |publisher=Survation |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029210941/https://www.survation.com/2013/05/ukip-won-in-8-westminster-constituencies-last-thursday/ |archive-date=29 October 2013 |access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref> UKIP performed strongly in and near the town of Boston, which was historically a safe Conservative area; this was seen as a surprise and was attributed to voters being concerned about immigration and feeling ignored by politicians.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/ukip/10037822/Why-did-voters-turn-to-Ukip-in-parts-of-true-blue-Lincolnshire.html |title=Why did voters turn to Ukip in parts of true blue Lincolnshire? |last=Mason |first=Rowena |date=4 May 2013 |work=The Daily Telegraph |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200108022908/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/ukip/10037822/Why-did-voters-turn-to-Ukip-in-parts-of-true-blue-Lincolnshire.html |url-status=live |archive-date=8 January 2020 |access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref> Afterwards, there was some media speculation that [[Nigel Farage]], the leader of UKIP, might stand in the constituency at the next general election; Simmonds said he "would be delighted" if Farage did, as it would give issues in the constituency more attention.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-22489993 |title=Tory MP Mark Simmonds would welcome Farage contest |last=Iredale |first=Tim |date=13 May 2013 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201173406/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-22489993 |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020}}</ref>
In the [[2014 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom|2014 European Parliament election]], which UKIP won ahead of Labour and the Conservatives, the Borough of Boston had the highest UKIP vote share in the country.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-27567744 |title=Farage: UKIP has 'momentum' and is targeting more victories |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=25 May 2014 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131213419/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-27567744 |url-status=live |archive-date=31 January 2020 |access-date=31 January 2020 |quote=Mr Farage has been celebrating his party's triumph in the European polls}}</ref><ref name=eu2014>{{cite web |url=https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/ukip-s-biggest-support-in-country-came-in-boston-and-now-it-is-set-to-be-key-election-target-1-6084203 |title=UKIP's biggest support in country came in Boston - and now it is set to be key election target |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=28 May 2014 |work=Boston Standard |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140531140154/https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/ukip-s-biggest-support-in-country-came-in-boston-and-now-it-is-set-to-be-key-election-target-1-6084203 |archive-date=31 May 2014 |access-date=31 January 2020 |quote=7,570 out of the 14,676 of the electorate who turned out [chose] UKIP}}</ref> The party gained 52% of votes in the borough, followed by the Conservatives and then Labour.<ref name=eu2014/> This led to the constituency being seen as a top target for UKIP in the next general election.<ref name=eu2014/>
On 11 August 2014, Simmonds resigned as a minister and announced that he would step down as the Member of Parliament for Boston and Skegness at the 2015 general election.<ref name=simmondsresings>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/11027010/Minister-quits-because-120000-salary-and-expenses-is-not-enough-to-support-his-family-in-London.html |title=Minister quits because £120,000 salary and expenses is not enough to support his family in London |last=Hope |first=Christopher |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |location=London |date=11 August 2014 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140812093314/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/11027010/Minister-quits-because-120000-salary-and-expenses-is-not-enough-to-support-his-family-in-London.html |url-status=live |archive-date=12 August 2014 |access-date=11 August 2014 }}</ref> Explaining his decision, he said that his salary and expenses of over £100,000 were not enough to maintain a home in London, which he said caused "intolerable" pressure in his family life.<ref name=simmondsresings/> This attracted some criticism, as Simmonds' salary was several times larger than the average salary in his constituency.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.spectator.com.au/2014/08/could-you-afford-to-become-an-mp/ |title=It costs £34,000 to become an MP. No wonder they expect higher pay |last=Hardman |first=Isabel |author-link=Isabel Hardman |date=16 August 2014 |work=[[The Spectator]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201181040/https://www.spectator.com.au/2014/08/could-you-afford-to-become-an-mp/ |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020 |quote=hearts will not be bleeding in his constituency, Boston and Skegness, where the average wage is £17,400}}</ref> There was also media speculation that he stood down due to the threat of UKIP gaining the seat.<ref name=simmondsresings/>
After Simmonds announced that he would not stand at the 2015 general election, the local Conservatives decided to select their candidate using the [[Conservative Party (UK) parliamentary primaries|open primary system]].<ref name=primarydetails>{{cite web |url=https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/details-revealed-of-boston-and-skegness-conservative-party-s-open-primary-1-6340009 |title=Details revealed of Boston and Skegness Conservative Party's 'open primary' |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=6 October 2014 |work=Boston Standard |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141015132444/https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/details-revealed-of-boston-and-skegness-conservative-party-s-open-primary-1-6340009 |url-status=dead |archive-date=15 October 2014 |quote=The local association has opted for an 'open primary' method of selection which offers the public the chance to vote on applicants}}</ref> Interviews were used to narrow down the number of applicants to four, with the winner then being chosen at a public meeting that all voters in the constituency could attend and vote in.<ref name=primarydetails/><ref name=shortlist>{{cite web |url=http://www.conservativehome.com/parliament/2014/10/the-final-four-in-the-boston-and-skegness-selection-are-named.html |title=The final four in the Boston and Skegness selection are named |last=Wallace |first=Mark |author-link=Mark Wallace (journalist) |date=20 October 2014 |website=[[ConservativeHome]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131153148/http://www.conservativehome.com/parliament/2014/10/the-final-four-in-the-boston-and-skegness-selection-are-named.html |url-status=live |archive-date=31 January 2020 |access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref> Several rounds of voting were used; the first two rounds, with 81 votes cast in each, both eliminated one candidate; the first candidate eliminated was [[Paul Bristow]], who later won the seat of [[Peterborough (UK Parliament constituency)|Peterborough]] in 2019.<ref name=warmanwon>{{cite web |url=https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/daily-telegraph-journalist-connects-with-conservatives-1-6379360 |title=Daily Telegraph journalist connects with Conservatives |last=Jaines |first=Daniel |date=25 October 2014 |work=Boston Standard |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141103155547/https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/daily-telegraph-journalist-connects-with-conservatives-1-6379360 |archive-date=3 November 2014 |access-date=31 January 2020 |quote=The head of technology at the Daily Telegraph has won the race to become the Boston and Skegness Conservative candidate for May 2015 in a hotly contested competition}}</ref> The third round saw 80 votes cast with a tie between the journalist [[Matt Warman]] and the headteacher Tim Clark.<ref name=shortlist/><ref name=warmanwon/> Another vote between the two was held, which was won by Warman, then the head of technology at ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]''.<ref name=warmanwon/> Warman, who was 33 at the time of the primary, argued that UKIP's support in the area was partly due to "a real disconnect between voters and politicians"; his wife's family lived in the constituency.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/open-primary-daily-telegraph-journalist-looking-to-connect-with-voters-1-6373411 |title=Open Primary: Daily Telegraph journalist looking to connect with voters |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=24 October 2014 |work=Boston Standard |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141109193154/https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/local/open-primary-daily-telegraph-journalist-looking-to-connect-with-voters-1-6373411 |archive-date=9 November 2014 |access-date=31 January 2020 |quote=Matt Warman, 33, has a strong affinity to the area, with wife Rachel's family living here}}</ref>
The seat had been one of UKIP's top target seats in that election.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/generalelection/general-election-2015-in-boston-ukip-hope-to-overturn-a-12000-vote-tory-majority-with-its-10156436.html |title=General Election 2015: In Boston, Ukip hope to overturn a 12,000-vote Tory majority with its immigration policies |last=Merill |first=Jamie |date=5 April 2015 |work=[[The Independent]] |access-date=9 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109175618/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/generalelection/general-election-2015-in-boston-ukip-hope-to-overturn-a-12000-vote-tory-majority-with-its-10156436.html |url-status=live |archive-date=9 January 2020 |quote="If we don't win this seat, we are not going to win many others," admitted the law graduate [Robin Hunter-Clarke]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/the-14-seats-most-likely-to-go-to-ukip-in-the-may-2015-general-election-2015-5?r=US&IR=T |title=The 14 seats most likely to go to UKIP in the May 2015 General Election |last=Hirst |first=Tomas |date=5 May 2015 |publisher=[[Business Insider]] |access-date=9 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109180100/https://www.businessinsider.com/the-14-seats-most-likely-to-go-to-ukip-in-the-may-2015-general-election-2015-5?r=US&IR=T |url-status=live |archive-date=9 January 2020 |quote=6. Boston and Skegness ... Verdict: This looked to be UKIP's best shot of adding to its seats, but its chances are slipping}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/11450075/Ukip-already-has-four-seats-in-the-bag-says-leading-expert-Matthew-Goodwin.html |title=Ukip already has four seats 'in the bag', says leading expert Matthew Goodwin |last=Hope |first=Christopher |date=4 March 2015 |publisher=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |access-date=9 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109180404/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/11450075/Ukip-already-has-four-seats-in-the-bag-says-leading-expert-Matthew-Goodwin.html |url-status=live |archive-date=9 January 2020 |quote=He [Goodwin] set out details of 10 seats ... which Ukip could win at May's election. They were: ... Boston and Skegness}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.channel4.com/news/ukip-farage-general-election-rotherham-seats |title=General election 2015: five seats Ukip could win |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= 6 February 2015 |publisher=[[Channel 4]] |access-date=9 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109180817/https://www.channel4.com/news/ukip-farage-general-election-rotherham-seats |url-status=live |archive-date=9 January 2020 |quote="It has a strong local branch, an active councillor in Robin Hunter-Clarke (pictured) and sits in Ukip's Lincolnshire heartland," Nottingham University Politics Professor Matthew Goodwin told Channel 4 News}}</ref> The journalist and commentator [[Iain Dale]] predicted in February 2015 that UKIP would gain the seat, writing "[if] UKIP are to make a breakthrough, it might well be here";{{sfn|Dale|2015|loc=Lincolnshire}} overall, Dale predicted that UKIP would make five gains at the election.{{sfn|Dale|2015|loc=The 5 UKIP Gains}} [[Opinion polling in United Kingdom constituencies, 2010–2015#Boston and Skegness|Two opinion polls]] of the constituency were carried out prior to the 2015 general election. A poll in September 2014 predicted a UKIP majority of 19%,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://survation.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Boston-Skegness-Results.pdf |title=Boston & Skegness Constituency Poll |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=27 September 2019 |publisher=[[Survation]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200130124314/https://survation.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Boston-Skegness-Results.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=30 January 2020 |access-date=30 January 2020}}</ref> while a 2015 poll forecast a narrow Conservative majority of 3%.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://lordashcroftpolls.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/Boston-Skegness-Feb-15-Full-tables.pdf |title=Boston & Skegness Poll |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=19 February 2015 |publisher=[[Michael Ashcroft#UK electoral polling|Lord Ashcroft Polls]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200130124635/http://lordashcroftpolls.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/Boston-Skegness-Feb-15-Full-tables.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=30 January 2020 |access-date=30 January 2020 |quote=Conservative 38% Labour 17% Liberal Democrat 5% UKIP 35%}}</ref> However, an internal poll conducted by UKIP (not released to the public) close to the election found a Conservative lead of seven points.{{sfn|Goodwin|Milazzo|2015|p=270}}
On the day of the election, 8 May 2015, Warman was duly elected as the Member of Parliament; the Conservative majority shrunk to 10% with the UKIP candidate [[Robin Hunter-Clarke]], a councillor on the [[Lincolnshire County Council]], coming in second place. Warman won 43.8% of the vote in the seat, while Hunter-Clarke achieved 33.8%, which was UKIP's second-highest vote share in any constituency in that election (after [[Clacton (UK Parliament constituency)|Clacton]], the only constituency the party won).{{sfn|Hawkins|Keen|Nakatudde|Ayres|2015|p=36}} UKIP increased their vote share by 24.3% compared to the previous general election, while the Conservative share of the vote fell by 5.7%; this was the seventh-largest increase in vote share achieved by UKIP at the election.{{sfn|Hawkins|Keen|Nakatudde|Ayres|2015|pp=36, 107}} Out of the 650 constituencies in the United Kingdom, the seat was the 126th most marginal in terms of percentage majority and 115th most marginal when measured by number of votes.{{sfn|Hawkins|Keen|Nakatudde|Ayres|2015|p=109}}

On 29 April 2017, [[Paul Nuttall]], the leader of UKIP at the time, announced that he was standing in Boston and Skegness, noting that the constituency had the highest Leave vote in the country.<ref>{{cite news|title=UKIP leader Paul Nuttall to stand in Boston and Skegness |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-39756016 |work=BBC News |date=29 April 2017 |access-date=12 January |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020 |quote=Mike Gilbert, 56, nominating officer and sole parliamentary candidate for A Blue Revolution}}</ref>
Nutall came in third place (with Labour second), winning just 7.7% of the vote; this was a decrease of 26.1% compared to 2015, and the third-largest percentage fall in UKIP vote share in that election.{{sfn|Baker|Hawkins|Audickas|Bate|2019|p=20}} UKIP's share of the vote fell nationally in that election, and the result was still their seventh-highest vote share of any seat.{{sfn|Baker|Hawkins|Audickas|Bate|2019|p=20}} The election saw UKIP achieve their worst result in the constituency since the 2001 general election. The Conservative majority increased to an all-time high in the seat, while Labour had their best result since 2005, achieving 25% of the votes cast. The Green Party and Liberal Democrats lost their deposits, mirroring the 2015 election results for both parties. Of the 46 constituencies in the [[East Midlands]] region, Boston and Skegness had the third lowest turnout at the election, at 62.7%.{{sfn|Uberoi|Baker|Cracknell|2019|p=29}}
Based on estimates produced by Professor [[Chris Hanretty]] of [[Royal Holloway, University of London]], Boston and Skegness had the third-highest vote share for the [[Brexit Party]] in the [[2019 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom|2019 European Parliament election]]. According to Hanretty, 56.4% of votes cast in the constituency were for the new anti-EU party, which was led by Farage, behind only [[Castle Point (UK Parliament constituency)|Castle Point]] and Clacton. Hanretty also estimated that the Conservatives came second in the seat, with 12.5% of the vote, followed by UKIP, who won 7.7%, their tenth strongest performance of the election. UKIP were closely followed by the Liberal Democrats and Labour, who came fourth and fifth with 7.5% and 7.4% of the vote respectively.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://medium.com/@chrishanretty/ep2019-results-mapped-onto-westminster-constituencies-8a2a6ed14146 |title=EP2019 results mapped onto Westminster constituencies |last=Hanretty |first=Chris |date=29 May 2019 |website=[[Medium (website)|Medium]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128132942/https://medium.com/@chrishanretty/ep2019-results-mapped-onto-westminster-constituencies-8a2a6ed14146 |url-status=live |archive-date=28 January 2020 |access-date=28 January 2020}}</ref>
The seat was discussed in 2019 as a potential target for the Brexit Party in the next general election, due to the high level of support for leaving the European Union in the constituency.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.co.uk/entry/brexit-automation-hunt-johnson_uk_5d1b56eae4b03d611642275d |title=Back £4bn Bid To Tackle Automation Threat, Tory Think-Tank Tells Hunt And Johnson |last=Wearmouth |first=Rachel |date=3 July 2019 |publisher=[[Huffington Post]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201204311/https://consent.yahoo.com/collectConsent?sessionId=2_cc-session_6dc972f2-9b90-4c01-a439-afb806494dee&lang=en-gb&inline=false |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020 |quote=Brexit Party target seats Corby, Boston and Skegness, Great Grimsby and Mansfield}}</ref> The Brexit Party achieved high levels of |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020 |quote=The Brexit party's support increased by two points to 26% of the vote in the latest Opinium poll}}</ref> and one estimate, by the website [[Electoral Calculus]], suggested that the Brexit Party would gain Boston and Skegness.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.lincolnshirelive.co.uk/news/local-news/shock-poll-predicts-brexit-party-3071088 |title=Shock poll predicts Brexit Party would sweep up seats in Lincolnshire in General Election However, the Brexit Party support decreased over time,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/brexit-party-poll-fade-corbyn-boris-bmg-a9000331.html |title=Brexit Party That's a lot of voters to persuade.}}</ref> [[Nigel Farage]] later announced that the Brexit Party would not stand in any constituency won by the Conservatives in 2017<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election-2019-50377396 |title=General election 2019: Brexit Party will not stand in Tory seats |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=11 November 2019 |work=[[BBC News]] |access-date=10 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200110110604/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election-2019-50377396 |url-status=live |archive-date=10 January 2020 |quote=The party will not now stand in 317 seats won by the Tories in 2017}}</ref> and the Brexit Party candidate would be [[Jonathan Bullock]], a [[Member of the European Parliament]] (MEP) for the [[East Midlands (European Parliament constituency)|East Midlands constituency]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/politics/brexit-party-u-turn-fighting-boston-and-skegness-seat-just-week-after-candidate-launched-campaign-925003 |title=Brexit Party in u-turn on fighting Boston and Skegness seat - just a week after candidate launched campaign |last=Holmes |first=Damian |date=12 November 2019 |work=Boston Standard |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200201175618/https://www.bostonstandard.co.uk/news/politics/brexit-party-u-turn-fighting-boston-and-skegness-seat-just-week-after-candidate-launched-campaign-925003 |url-status=live |archive-date=1 February 2020 |access-date=1 February 2020}}</ref> UKIP did not stand in the constituency. They stood in only 44 out of 650 British seats at the election.{{sfn|Uberoi|Baker|Cracknell|2019|pp=8–9, 22}} In the election, held on 12 December, the Conservatives further increased their majority, winning 76.7% of the vote.{{sfn|Uberoi|Baker|Cracknell|2019|p=10}} This was the Conservatives' second-highest vote share in the election (after Castle Point).{{sfn|Uberoi|Baker|Cracknell|2019|p=10}} The seat was also the fifteenth safest seat in the election (measured by percentage majority) and the second-safest Conservative seat after neighbouring South Holland and the Deepings.{{sfn|Uberoi|Baker|Cracknell|2019|p=73}}

{{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 1885 onwards}} {{For|the Canadian electoral districts in [[Ontario]]|Lincoln (federal electoral district)|Lincoln (provincial electoral district)}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}} {{Use British English|date=June 2020}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Lincoln |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Lincoln (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East Midlands - Lincoln constituency.svg|175px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Lincoln in the East Midlands |year = 1265 |abolished = |type = Borough |elects_howmany = Two until 1885, then one |previous = |next = |electorate = 74,128 (2023){{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-east-midlands/#lg_lincoln-bc-74128 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – East Midlands |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=2 July 2024 |df=dmy }} |mp = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |party = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |region = England |county = [[Lincolnshire]] |towns = [[Lincoln, Lincolnshire|Lincoln]] }} '''Lincoln''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[borough constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} in [[Lincolnshire]], [[England]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since 2019 by [[Karl McCartney]], a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] politician.{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} Since the split of the [[City of York (UK Parliament constituency)|City of York]] seat with effect from the 2010 general election, Lincoln has been the oldest constituency in continuous existence in the UK – established in 1265. Lincoln was a [[bellwether]] between 1974 and 2017. The seat bucked the national Conservative victory in 1970 by electing a Labour MP, as it did in 2017. The seat has been considered relative to others an ultra-marginal seat, as well as a swing seat, since 2005 as its winner's majority has not exceeded 6.9% of the vote since the 12.5% majority won in 2005 and the seat has changed hands three times since that year. ==Boundaries== '''1885–1918''': The existing parliamentary borough, and the parish of Bracebridge.{{cite book |author= |title=The Public General Acts of the United Kingdom passed in the forty-eighth and forty-ninth years of the reign of Queen Victoria |url=https://archive.org/details/publicgeneralac01walegoog |location=London |publisher=Eyre and Spottiswoode |pages=[https://archive.org/details/publicgeneralac01walegoog/page/n114 111]–198 |date=1885 |chapter=Chap. 23. Redistribution of Seats Act, 1885 }} '''1918–1950''': The County Borough of Lincoln, and the Urban District of Bracebridge. '''1950–1974''': The County Borough of Lincoln. '''1974–1983''': As prior but with redrawn boundaries. '''1983–1997''': The City of Lincoln, and the District of North Kesteven wards of Bracebridge Heath, North Hykeham Central, North Hykeham North, North Hykeham South, Skellingthorpe, and Waddington West. '''1997–2010''': The City of Lincoln, and the District of North Kesteven ward of Bracebridge Heath. '''2010–2024''': The City of Lincoln, and the District of North Kesteven wards of Bracebridge Heath and Waddington East, and Skellingthorpe. '''2024–present''': Following a local government boundary review in the District of North Kesteven which came into effect in May 2023,{{Cite web |last=LGBCE |title=North Kesteven {{!}} LGBCE |url=https://www.lgbce.org.uk/all-reviews/north-kesteven |access-date=2024-04-09 |website=www.lgbce.org.uk |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=The North Kesteven (Electoral Changes) Order 2021 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2021/1052/contents/made}} the constituency now comprises the following: * The City Of Lincoln. * In the District of Kesteven: the Bracebridge Heath ward; the majority of the Skellingthorpe & Eagle ward; and the majority of the Waddington Rural ward.{{Cite web |title=New Seat Details - Lincoln |url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/calcwork23.py?seat=Lincoln |access-date=2024-04-09 |website=www.electoralcalculus.co.uk}} Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency (based on the ward structure which existed on 1 December 2020) is unchanged.{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule 1 Part 1 East Midlands}} The constituency, as its name suggests, covers the [[cathedral city]]{{#tag:ref|[[Lincoln Cathedral]] was from 1311 until an intense storm in 1549 [[List of tallest church buildings in the world|the world's tallest building]] |group= n}} of [[Lincoln, Lincolnshire|Lincoln]] in [[Lincolnshire]], and most of its directly adjoining villages. ==History== Lincoln first sent Members to Parliament in 1265, thirty years before the first all-over coverage of cities and qualifying towns was introduced in the [[Model Parliament]], and has done so ever since, although no records exist from before the end of the 13th century. The early elections were held at the Guildhall and the [[burgess (title)|burgess]]es elected were usually officials of the borough. The representation, originally two Members ("burgesses"), was reduced to one Member in 1885. The seat was represented for five years by former Cabinet minister [[Margaret Beckett|Margaret Jackson, later Margaret Beckett]].{{#tag:ref|Changed seat in 1983 to serve [[Derby South (UK Parliament constituency)|Derby South]] which she has held to date (winning most recently in 2019)|group= n}} Lincoln became the oldest constituency in the country in 2010 when the [[City of York (UK Parliament constituency)|City of York constituency]] was divided. ==Constituency profile== The seat includes the [[University of Lincoln]]. From 1945 to 1972 Lincoln was continuously held by the Labour Party, often as a [[safe seat]]. The city has good transport links with [[Nottingham]], [[Kingston upon Hull|Hull]] and the smaller ancient market towns in [[Lincolnshire]], such as [[Spalding, Lincolnshire|Spalding]], [[Market Rasen]] and [[Boston, Lincolnshire|Boston]]. Lincoln was a [[bellwether constituency]] from October 1974 to [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015]], voting for the party which would form the government in each election. '''Northampton North''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[borough constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024]] by [[Lucy Rigby]], a member of [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} The constituency is a considered a [[bellwether]], as it has reflected the national result at every general election since it was created in [[February 1974 United Kingdom general election|February 1974]].
==History== This constituency was created for the election of [[February 1974 United Kingdom general election|February 1974]] when the [[Northampton (UK Parliament constituency)|old constituency of Northampton]] was split into Northampton North and [[Northampton South (UK Parliament constituency)|Northampton South]].
Since creation it has been a bellwether, electing an MP from the winning (or largest governing) party in every general election.
==Boundaries==
=== Historic === '''1974–1983''': The County Borough of Northampton wards of Abington, Dallington, Kingsthorpe, Park, St David, and St George.<ref>{{cite legislation UK|type=si|si=The Parliamentary Constituencies (Daventry, Wellingborough and Northampton) Order 1973|year=1973|number=604|accessdate=26 February 2023}}</ref>
'''1983–2010''': The Borough of Northampton wards of Abington, Boughton Green, Dallington and Kings Heath, Headlands, Kingsthorpe, Lings, Lumbertubs, Park, St Alban, St George, Thorplands, and Welford.
'''2010–2024''': The Borough of Northampton wards of Abington, Boughton Green, Eastfield, Headlands, Kingsley, Kingsthorpe, Lumbertubs, Parklands, St David, and Thorplands.
''NB: with effect from 1 April 2021, the Borough of Northampton was abolished and absorbed into the new unitary authority of West Northamptonshire.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Northamptonshire (Structural Changes) Order 2020 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2020/156/contents}}</ref>''
=== Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 April 2021):
* The District of West Northamptonshire wards of: Abington and Phippsville; Boothville and Parklands; Castle; Dallington Spencer; Headlands; Kingsthorpe North; Kingsthorpe South; St. George; Talavera.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part I}}</ref>
''The constituency was expanded considerably with the addition of Northampton town centre from [[Northampton South (UK Parliament constituency)|Northampton South]].''
==Constituency profile== The constituency has income, [[social housing]] and unemployment statistics<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2010/nov/17/unemployment-and-employment-statistics-economics Unemployment claimants by constituency] ''[[The Guardian]]''</ref> close to the national average. There is a varied and dynamic service and engineering-centred economy typical of the [[East Midlands]], with significant foodstuffs, clothing and consumables manufacturing and processing operations.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html|title=2011 Census Interactive - ONS|work=ons.gov.uk|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129132219/http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html|archive-date=2016-01-29}}</ref> Health inequality is high, with the life expectancy gap between the least deprived and most deprived men in Northampton reaching over a decade.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/health-profiles/2019/e07000154.html?area-name=northampton|title=E07000154|website=fingertips.phe.org.uk}}</ref> According to [[Public Health England]], the constituency is "considerably worse than [the] England average" in terms of violent crime, self harm, [[Teenage pregnancy in the United Kingdom|under 18 conception]] and [[General Certificate of Secondary Education|GCSE]] achievement.<ref name="auto"/>

{{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 2010 onwards}} {{For|the constituency in the south of Northampton|Northampton South (UK Parliament constituency)}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = South Northamptonshire |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/South Northamptonshire (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East Midlands - South Northamptonshire constituency.svg|175px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of South Northamptonshire in the East Midlands |year = 2010 |abolished = |type = County |previous = [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]] |next = |elects_howmany = One |year2 = 1950 |abolished2 = [[February 1974 United Kingdom general election|1974]] |previous2 = [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]] and [[Kettering (UK Parliament constituency)|Kettering]] |next2 = [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]] |elects_howmany2 = One |year3 = 1832 |abolished3 = 1918 |elects_howmany3 = 1832–1885: Two
1885–1918: One |previous3 = [[Northamptonshire (UK Parliament constituency)|Northamptonshire]] |next3 = [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]] |electorate = 76,555 (2023){{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-east-midlands/#lg_south-northamptonshire-cc-76555 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – East Midlands |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=3 July 2024 |df=dmy }} |mp = Sarah Bool |party = [[Conservative Party|Conservative]] |region = England |county = [[Northamptonshire]] |towns = [[Brackley]], [[King's Sutton]], [[Towcester]] }} '''South Northamptonshire''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since its 2010 recreation by [[Andrea Leadsom]], a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] who served as [[Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy]] until 13 February 2020. She was [[Leader of the House of Commons]] from 2017 to 2019, and [[Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] from 2016 to 2017. {{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} The seat of South Northamptonshire is considered a Conservative safe seat, having elected a Conservative MP at every election for 110 Years. Current Conservative MP [[Andrea Leadsom]] was re-elected in 2019 with an increased majority. In May 2024, she announced that she would stand down as an MP at the up-coming [[2024 United Kingdom general election|general election]].{{cite web |title=Michael Gove and Andrea Leadsom to stand down at general election |url=https://amp.theguardian.com/politics/article/2024/may/24/michael-gove-to-stand-down-at-general-election}} ==Constituency profile== This is a rural seat around [[Towcester]] and [[Brackley]]. There is a significant motorsport sector including [[Silverstone Circuit|Silverstone]].UK Polling Report http://ukpollingreport.co.uk/2015guide/northamptonshiresouth/ Incomes and house prices are above average for the UK.Electoral Calculus https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/seatdetails.py?seat=Northamptonshire+South ==History== Before [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010]], the constituency existed from 1832 to 1918, and from 1950 to 1974, however on different boundaries during each period. It elected two [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Members of Parliament]] (MPs) by the [[Plurality-at-large voting|bloc vote]] system of [[election]] from 1832, until the representation was reduced in 1885 to one member elected by the [[first past the post]] system. ;Prominent members Three names feature prominently among the area's Commons members, the [[John Spencer, 3rd Earl Spencer|3rd]] and [[John Spencer, 5th Earl Spencer|5th]] [[Earl Spencer (peerage)|Earl Spencer]] (during their tenures as MP having a courtesy title only, Viscount Althorp – [[Althorp]] is a major country house in the seat, well known as the childhood home of [[Diana, Princess of Wales]]); [[Edward Fitzroy]] (son of [[Baron Southampton|Lord Southampton]]), [[Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)|Speaker of the House of Commons]] from 1928 until his death in 1943; and lastly, [[Reginald Manningham-Buller, 1st Viscount Dilhorne]] who on accomplishment of a peerage sat for the final two years of his life as the historic equivalent of the [[President of the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom]] with additional functions, the [[Lord Chancellor]]. In the 19th century history of the seat the Cartwright family (with three members) lived in the stately home [[Aynhoe Park]] near [[Banbury]]. ;History of boundaries The seat was abolished in 1918 to form the new constituency of [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]], then recreated in 1950 caused by a relatively short-lived abolition of Daventry. In 1974 the constituency was almost wholly swallowed up by a reborn Daventry, which on wide boundaries saw substantial population growth. This called for recreation in 2010 whereby most of the electoral wards were taken from the former version of the [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]] seat. ;Present bordering constituencies The constituency is bordered by [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]] and [[Northampton South (UK Parliament constituency)|Northampton South]] to the north, [[Wellingborough (UK Parliament constituency)|Wellingborough]] to the north east, [[Milton Keynes North (UK Parliament constituency)|Milton Keynes North]] and [[Milton Keynes South (UK Parliament constituency)|Milton Keynes South]] to the south east, [[Buckingham (UK Parliament constituency)|Buckingham]] to the south, [[Banbury (UK Parliament constituency)|Banbury]] to the south west and [[Kenilworth and Southam (UK Parliament constituency)|Kenilworth and Southam]] to the west. ==Boundaries== === Historic === '''1832–1885''': The Hundreds of Kings Sutton, Chipping Warden, Greens Norton, Cleley, Towcester, Fawsley, Wymersley, Spelhoe, Nobottle Grove, and Guilsborough.{{Cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Uq0uAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA300 |title=The statutes of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. 2 & 3 William IV. Cap. LXIV. An Act to settle and describe the Divisions of Counties, and the Limits of Cities and Boroughs, in England and Wales, in so far as respects the Election of Members to serve in Parliament.|location= London |publisher=His Majesty's statute and law printers |date=1832 |pages=300–383 |access-date=23 May 2020}} '''1885–1918''': The Sessional Divisions of Brackley and Towcester, and part of the Sessional Division of Daventry. ''(The part of the Sessional Division of Daventry included in South Northamptonshire excluded the parishes of Ashby St. Ledgers, Barby, Claycoton Crick, Elkington, Kilsby, Lilboume, Long Buckley, Stanford, Watford, West Haddon, Winwick, and Yelvertoft, which were assigned to [[Mid Northamptonshire (UK Parliament constituency)|Mid Northamptonshire]]).'' {{Cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/publicgeneralac01walegoog/page/n169/mode/2up?view=theater|title= The statutes of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. 48 & 49 Victoria. Ch. 23: Redistribution of Seats Act 1885, Schedule 7.|location= London |publisher= His Majesty's statute and law printers |date= 1885 |pages= 166–167 |access-date=2023-12-19}} '''1950–1974''': The Boroughs of Daventry and Brackley, and the Rural Districts of Brackley, Daventry, Northampton, and Towcester. '''2010–2021''': The District of South Northamptonshire wards of Astwell, Blakesley, Blisworth, Brackley East, Brackley South, Brackley West, Chase, Cogenhoe, Collingtree, Cosgrove, Courteenhall, Deanshanger, Grafton, Kings Sutton, Kingthorn, Little Brook, Middleton Cheney, Salcey, Silverstone, Steane, Tove, Towcester Brook, Towcester Mill, Wardoun, Washington, Whittlewood, and Yardley, and the Borough of Northampton wards of East Hunsbury, Nene Valley, and West Hunsbury. '''2021–2024''': With effect from 1 April 2021, the Borough of Northampton and the District of South Northamptonshire were abolished and absorbed into the new unitary authority of West Northamptonshire.{{Cite web |title=The Northamptonshire (Structural Changes) Order 2020 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2020/156/contents}} From that date, the constituency comprised the District of West Northamptonshire wards of Brackley, Bugbrooke (part), Deanshanger, Duston West and St. Crispin (part), East Hunsbury and Shelfleys, Hackleton and Grange Park, Middleton Cheney, Nene Valley, Silverstone, Sixfields (part), and Towcester and Roade. === Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 April 2021): * The District of North Northamptonshire ward of Irchester (polling districts WAA, WAB, WPA, WPB and WPC) * The District of West Northamptonshire wards of Brackley; Bugbrooke; Deanshanger; Hackleton and Grange Park; Middleton Cheney; Silverstone (polling districts SAA, SAB, SAN, SAT, SBP, SBX, SCV, SDG, SDW, SDZ, SEF, SEW, SFE, SFF, SFN, SFO, SFR, SFW, SGD, SGF and SGK); Towcester and Roade.{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part I}} ''The parts in the former Borough of Northampton were transferred to [[Northampton South (UK Parliament constituency)|Northampton South]]. The constituency gained the part of the Irchester ward from [[Wellingborough (UK Parliament constituency)|Wellingborough]] and the remainder of the Bugbrooke ward from [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]]. A small part of Silverstone ward was transferred to Daventry.'' == Members of Parliament == === MPs 1832–1885 === ''[[Northamptonshire (UK Parliament constituency)|Northamptonshire]] prior to 1832'' {| class="wikitable" |- !Election!!colspan="2"|1st Member{{Rayment-hc|n|3|date=March 2012}}{{cite web|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/constituencies/northamptonshire-southern|title=Northamptonshire Southern 1832-1918 (Hansard)|website=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]}} !1st Party!!colspan="2"|2nd Member!!2nd Party |- | [[1832 United Kingdom general election|1832]] | rowspan="2" style="background-color: {{party color|Whigs (British political party)}}" | | rowspan="2" | [[John Spencer, 3rd Earl Spencer|Viscount Althorp]] | rowspan="2" | [[Whigs (British political party)|Whig]]{{cite book |last=Stooks Smith |first=Henry. |editor=Craig, F.
