{{short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 1918 onwards}} {{Use British English|date=August 2015}} {{Use dmy dates|date=August 2015}} {{Infobox UK constituency |name = Wellingborough and Rushden |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Wellingborough and Rushden (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East Midlands - Wellingborough and Rushden constituency.svg|175px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Wellingborough and Rushden in the East Midlands |year = 1918 |abolished = |type = County |previous = [[East Northamptonshire (UK Parliament constituency)|East Northamptonshire]] and [[North Northamptonshire (UK Parliament constituency)|North Northamptonshire]] |next = |electorate = 76,669 (2023)<ref>{{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-east-midlands/#lg_wellingborough-and-rushden-cc-76669 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – East Midlands |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=3 July 2024 |df=dmy }}</ref> |mp = [[Gen Kitchen(politician)|Gen Kitchen]] |party = Labour |region = England |county = [[Northamptonshire]] |towns = [[Wellingborough]], [[Rushden]], [[Higham Ferrers]], [[Irchester]] and [[Finedon]] |original_name=Wellingborough}}
'''Wellingborough and Rushden''' is a [[Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom|constituency]] in [[Northamptonshire]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[UK Parliament]]. The seat is currently held by [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|MP]] [[Gen Kitchen]], after the [[Recall of MPs Act 2015|recall]] of MP [[Peter Bone]] in December 2023 which resulted in [[2024 Wellingborough by-election|a by-election]] in February 2024.
Prior to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], the constituency was known as '''Wellingborough''' up until the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume one: Report – East Midlands {{!}} Boundary Commission for England |url=https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/2023-review-volume-one-report/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-one-report-east-midlands/ |access-date=2023-07-25 |website=boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk}}</ref>
==History== This seat was created under the [[Representation of the People Act 1918]].
;Political history Wellingborough's earliest years were [[Left-wing politics|left-leaning]]. Between 1964 and 2005, the seat kept on producing examples of [[bellwether]] results and rarely showed itself to be [[Safe seat|safe]] for more than one government term. Departing from this are two years where the result has defied the most common result nationwide, by leaning towards the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], in 1974 (twice). Since 2010 it became a safe seat for the Conservatives until the 2024 by-election.
In the [[2016 EU referendum]], Wellingborough voted 62.4% leave (25,679 votes) to 37.6% remain (15,462 votes)<ref>{{cite web |title=EU Referendum local results – W |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/politics/eu_referendum/results/local/w |publisher=BBC News}}</ref>
;Prominent frontbenchers [[Sir Geoffrey Shakespeare, 1st Baronet|Sir Geoffrey Shakespeare]] was a Lloyd-Georgist [[National Liberal Party (UK, 1922)|National Liberal]] who served in junior ministerial roles through much of the [[Second World War]], including briefly as the Secretary for Overseas Trade in 1940.
==Boundaries==
=== Historic (Wellingborough) === {{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Wellingborough (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame=yes|frame-height=250|text=Map of boundaries 2010-2024}} '''1918–1950''': The Borough of Higham Ferrers, the Urban Districts of Finedon, Irthlingborough, Raunds, Rushden, and Wellingborough, the Rural District of Wellingborough, and in the Rural District of Thrapston the parishes of Chelveston cum Caldecott, Hargrave, and Stanwick.
'''1950–1974''': The Borough of Higham Ferrers, the Urban Districts of Irthlingborough, Raunds, Rushden, and Wellingborough, the Rural District of Wellingborough, and in the Rural District of Oundle and Thrapston the civil parishes of Chelveston cum Caldecott and Hargrave.
'''1974–1983''': The Borough of Higham Ferrers, the Urban Districts of Irthlingborough, Oundle, Raunds, Rushden, and Wellingborough, and the Rural Districts of Oundle and Thrapston, and Wellingborough.<ref>{{cite legislation UK |type=si |si=The Parliamentary Constituencies (Daventry, Wellingborough and Northampton) Order 1973 |year=1973 |number=604 |access-date=26 February 2023}}</ref>
'''1983–2010''': The Borough of Wellingborough, and the District of East Northamptonshire wards of Higham Ferrers, Rushden East, Rushden North, Rushden South, and Rushden West.
'''2010–2021''': The Borough of Wellingborough wards of Brickhill, Castle, Croyland, Finedon, Great Doddington and Wilby, Hemmingwell, Irchester, North, Queensway, Redwell East, Redwell West, South, Swanspool, and Wollaston, and the District of East Northamptonshire wards of Higham Ferrers, Rushden East, Rushden North, Rushden South, and Rushden West.
'''2021–2024''': With effect from 1 April 2021, the Borough of Wellingborough and the District of East Northamptonshire were abolished and absorbed into the new unitary authority of North Northamptonshire.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Northamptonshire (Structural Changes) Order 2020 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2020/156/contents}}</ref> From that date, the constituency comprised the District of North Northamptonshire wards of Brickhill and Queensway, Croyland and Swanspool; Earls Barton (part), Finedon, Hatton Park, Higham Ferrers, Irchester, Irthlingborough, Rushden Pemberton West and Rushden South.
=== Current (Wellingborough and Rushden) === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 April 2021):
* The District of North Northamptonshire wards of: Brickhill and Queensway; Croyland and Swanspool; Finedon; Hatton Park; Higham Ferrers; Irchester (polling districts WIA and WIB); Irthlingborough (polling districts SD and SF); Rushden Pemberton West; Rushden South.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule 1 Part 1 East Midlands}}</ref>
''The parts of the Earls Barton ward were transferred to [[Daventry (UK Parliament constituency)|Daventry]]. In addition, parts of the Irchester ward were transferred to [[South Northamptonshire (UK Parliament constituency)|South Northamptonshire]], whilst the parts of the Irthlingborough ward were transferred in from [[Corby (UK Parliament constituency)|Corby]].''
The constituency is named after the towns of [[Wellingborough]] and [[Rushden]]. It also includes the small town of [[Higham Ferrers]], which was itself a [[borough constituency]] until its abolition as one of the [[rotten boroughs]] in 1832.
==Constituency profile== Strengths in local industries here or in neighbouring [[Northampton]] and [[Kettering]] include in printing, logistics and distribution, automotive (assembly and design), construction, food processing and advanced engineering sectors. Despite this, a decline in the traditional local industries such as quarrying, furniture making and textiles pushes workless claimants who were registered jobseekers in November 2012 higher than the national (and regional) average of 3.8%, at 4.5% of the population based on a statistical compilation by ''[[The Guardian]]''.<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2010/nov/17/unemployment-and-employment-statistics-economics Unemployment claimants by constituency] ''[[The Guardian]]''</ref>

==Constituency profile== On average earners' incomes are slightly lower than the national average<ref>{{cite web |url=http://neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk |title=2001 Census |publisher=Office for National Statistics |access-date=28 December 2014 }}</ref> and in 2010 unemployment stood at 7.4%, which was higher than the East Midlands average at the time of 3.6%<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2010/nov/17/unemployment-and-employment-statistics-economics |title=Unemployment: the key UK data and benefit claimants for every constituency |date= 15 May 2013 |author=Simon Rogers, John Burn-Murdoch and Ami Sedghi |work=The Guardian |access-date=28 December 2014 }}</ref> however the picture is not uniform across all 2011 Census Output Areas, some of which have incomes at the national average or above and together with the affordability of property in the area, those on the national average way or above generally have the ability to save, purchase property or enjoy a high standard of living.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html |title=2011 census interactive maps |publisher=Office for National Statistics |access-date=28 December 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129132219/http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html |archive-date=29 January 2016 |df=dmy-all }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mouseprice.com/area-guide/ng3 |title=NG3 (Nottingham) area guide |publisher=Mouseprice |access-date=28 December 2014 }}</ref>
==Boundaries== === Historic === '''1885–1918''': The Borough of Nottingham wards of Byron, Manvers, Mapperley, Robin Hood, and St Ann's.
'''1918–1950''': The County Borough of Nottingham wards of Byron, Manvers, Mapperley, and St Mary's.
'''1950–1955''': The County Borough of Nottingham wards of Byron, Manvers, Mapperley, and St Ann's.
'''1974–1983''': The County Borough of Nottingham wards of Bridge, Lenton, Manvers, Market, St Ann's, and Trent.
'''1983–2010''': The City of Nottingham wards of Basford, Forest, Greenwood, Manvers, Mapperley, Radford, St Ann's, Sherwood, and Trent.
'''2010–2024''': The City of Nottingham wards of Arboretum, Berridge, Dales, Mapperley, St Ann's, and Sherwood.
=== Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 December 2020):
* The City of Nottingham wards of Berridge, Castle, Dales, Hyson Green & Arboretum, Mapperley, St Ann's, and Sherwood.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule 1 Part 1 East Midlands}}</ref>
''The Castle ward, which incorporates Nottingham city centre was transferred from [[Nottingham South (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham South]].''
The constituency covers the north-eastern part of the City of [[Nottingham]]. It includes the suburbs of [[Mapperley]], [[Carrington, Nottingham|Carrington]] and [[Sherwood, Nottingham|Sherwood]], and the inner city areas of [[Hyson Green]], [[St Ann's, Nottingham|St Ann's]], [[Bakersfield, Nottingham|Bakersfield]] and [[Sneinton]].
==History== The present Nottingham East constituency was created in 1974, and first elected Jack Dunnett who had been Labour MP for the abolished [[Nottingham Central (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham Central]] seat. [[Michael Knowles (politician)|Michael Knowles]] regained it for the Conservative Party in 1983, when some of the seat was transferred to the new [[Nottingham South (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham South]] constituency in [[Boundary commissions (United Kingdom)|boundary changes]]. Knowles held the seat with a reduced majority in 1987, but [[John Heppell]] gained it for Labour in 1992, and held the seat until he retired in 2010. Until 2019 it was held by Chris Leslie, initially for Labour Co-operative and later for Change UK. Leslie previously represented his hometown constituency of [[Shipley (UK Parliament constituency)|Shipley]] in West Yorkshire, from 1997 until losing his seat to [[Philip Davies]] in 2005. During his first term he joined the [[frontbencher|front benches]] serving as a junior minister as part of the [[Premiership of Tony Blair|Tony Blair Government]] and was briefly [[Shadow Chancellor]] after the 2015 general election. The incumbent MP, [[Nadia Whittome]], is the current [[Baby of the House#United Kingdom|Baby of the House]], aged 23 upon her election in [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019]].

{{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 1885 onwards}} {{EngvarB|date=June 2016}} {{Use dmy dates|date=June 2016}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Newark |parliament = uk |image={{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Newark (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East Midlands - Newark constituency.svg|175px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Newark in the East Midlands |map_entity = [[Nottinghamshire]] |map_year = |year = 1885 |abolished = |type = County |elects_howmany = One |year2 = 1673 |abolished2 = 1885 |type2 = Borough |elects_howmany2 = Two |electorate = 76,478 (2023)<ref>{{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-east-midlands/#lg_newark-cc-76478 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – East Midlands |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=3 July 2024 |df=dmy }}</ref> |mp = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |party = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |region = [[England]] |county = [[Nottinghamshire]] |towns = [[Newark-on-Trent]], [[Southwell, Nottinghamshire|Southwell]] }} '''Newark''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} in [[Nottinghamshire]], [[United Kingdom|England]]. It was most recently represented by [[Robert Jenrick]] of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], prior to the dissoluton of Parliament, who won the seat in a [[2014 Newark by-election|by-election]] on 5 June 2014, following the resignation of [[Patrick Mercer]] in April 2014.{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one Member of Parliament (MP) by the [[first-past-the-post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}}
== Boundaries == === Historic === '''1918–1950''': The Municipal Borough of Newark, and the Rural Districts of Bingham, Newark, and Southwell.
'''1950–1955''': The Municipal Borough of Newark, the Urban District of Mansfield Woodhouse, and the Rural Districts of Newark and Southwell.<ref>{{Cite legislation UK |type=act |year=1948 |chapter=65 |act=Representation of the People Act 1948 |schedule=1 |accessdate=23 July 2023 }}</ref>
'''1955–1983''': The Municipal Borough of Newark, and the Rural Districts of Newark and Southwell.<ref>{{cite book |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=1956 |title=Statutory Instruments 1955 |series=Part II |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8TDyAAAAMAAJ |chapter=The Parliamentary Constituencies (Nottinghamshire) Order 1955. SI 1955/169 |location=London |publisher=[[Her Majesty's Stationery Office]] |pages=2157–2159 |isbn=}}</ref>
'''1983–2010''': The District of Newark wards of Beacon, Bridge, Bullpit Pinfold, Castle, Caunton, Collingham, Devon, Elston, Farndon, Magnus, Meering, Milton Lowfield, Muskham, Southwell East, Southwell West, Sutton on Trent, Trent, and Winthorpe, and the District of Bassetlaw wards of East Markham, East Retford East, East Retford North, East Retford West, Elkesley, Trent, and Tuxford.
'''2010–2024''': The District of Newark and Sherwood wards of Balderton North, Balderton West, Beacon, Bridge, Castle, Caunton, Collingham and Meering, Devon, Farndon, Lowdham, Magnus, Muskham, Southwell East, Southwell North, Southwell West, Sutton-on-Trent, Trent, and Winthorpe, the District of Bassetlaw wards of East Markham, Rampton, Tuxford, and Trent, and the Borough of Rushcliffe wards of Bingham East, Bingham West, Cranmer, Oak, and Thoroton.
=== Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency was defined as follows (as they existed on 1 December 2020):
* The District of Bassetlaw wards of: Clayworth; East Markham; Rampton; Sturton; Tuxford and Trent. * The District of Newark & Sherwood wards of: Balderton North & Coddington; Balderton South; Beacon; Bridge; Castle; Collingham; Devon; Farndon & Fernwood; Muskham; Southwell; Sutton-on-Trent; Trent. * The Borough of Rushcliffe wards of: Bingham East; Bingham West; Cranmer; East Bridgford; Thoroton.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part I}}</ref> <sup>1</sup>
''The constituency saw minor boundary changes, primarily due to the redrawing of local authority ward boundaries.''
<sup>1</sup> Following a further local government boundary review which came into effect in May 2023,<ref>{{Cite web |last=LGBCE |title=Rushcliffe {{!}} LGBCE |url=https://www.lgbce.org.uk/all-reviews/rushcliffe |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.lgbce.org.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Rushcliffe (Electoral Changes) Order 2022 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2022/1364/contents/made}}</ref> the parts in the Borough of Rushcliffe now comprise the following wards from the 2024 general election:
* Bingham North; Bingham South; Cranmer; East Bridgford; Newton (majority); and a small part of Nevile & Langar.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Seat Details - Newark |url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/calcwork23.py?seat=Newark |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.electoralcalculus.co.uk}}</ref> The constituency covers large parts of the [[Newark and Sherwood]] district which encompasses the east of [[Nottinghamshire]], as such includes the towns of [[Newark-on-Trent]] and [[Southwell, Nottinghamshire|Southwell]], and the villages of [[Collingham, Nottinghamshire|Collingham]] and [[Sutton-on-Trent]]. It also covers parts of the [[Bassetlaw District|Bassetlaw]] and [[Rushcliffe]] areas including [[Markham Moor]] and [[Bingham, Nottinghamshire|Bingham]].
== History ==
Newark was the last borough to be added to the [[Unreformed House of Commons]] which took place in 1673, prior to the [[Reform Act 1832]]. It returned two representatives to [[Parliament of England|Parliament]] from 1673 until 1885.
Newark petitioned for enfranchisement as a [[parliamentary borough]] in the 1660s, in recognition of the town's royalist sympathies during the [[English Civil War]]. It was eventually enfranchised by a royal charter in early 1673, which gave the rights of election to the mayor and aldermen. However, the freemen of the town contested this, and held a separate election in which they selected a different member to the aldermen. The dispute in Parliament lasted until 1677, when the charter was withdrawn and a new one issued, causing a fresh election in which all inhabitants paying [[scot and lot]] could vote. In 1685, a third charter was issued, giving the right of election to all [[forty-shilling freeholders]].<ref>[http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1660-1690/constituencies/newark History of Parliament: Newark: 1660-1690]</ref> The borough constituency existed until 1885, when it was replaced by a county division of the same name under the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]].
The future Prime Minister, [[William Ewart Gladstone]], began his political career as Member of Parliament for Newark from 1832 to 1845. More recently, the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] held Newark (on substantially different boundaries to the present ones) from 1950 until 1979, when it was taken by the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]]' [[Richard Alexander (UK politician)|Richard Alexander]]. Alexander lost his seat during Labour's landslide victory at the [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997 general election]]. The victorious Labour candidate, [[Fiona Jones]], was convicted of [[electoral fraud]] and expelled from the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] in 1999 over misrepresented election expenses. The conviction was later overturned upon appeal and she returned to Parliament. However, Jones lost her seat at the [[2001 United Kingdom general election|2001 general election]] to [[Patrick Mercer]] of the Conservatives, who held it until 2014.
Mercer held the position of Shadow Minister for Homeland Security from June 2003 until March 2007, when he was forced to resign following racially contentious comments made to ''[[The Times]]''.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/politics/article1484909.ece | location=London | work=The Times | first=David | last=Byers | title=Exclusive Tory frontbencher sparks race row with black bastards gibe | date=8 March 2007}}</ref>
The Newark constituency in 2010 lost the town of [[Retford]] to the [[Bassetlaw (UK Parliament constituency)|Bassetlaw]] constituency (although Newark still has a smaller part of the Bassetlaw district), but gained land in and around [[Bingham, Nottinghamshire|Bingham]] from the [[Rushcliffe (UK Parliament constituency)|Rushcliffe]] constituency, thus making it much safer Conservative territory.
Following an investigation by Commons authorities finding that Mr Mercer had engaged in paid lobbying, not properly reported the income or declared his interest, and repeatedly seriously denigrated other members, Patrick Mercer stepped down as MP for Newark on 30 April 2014.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-27208966 | work=BBC | title=Former Tory MP Mercer resigns after Commons suspension | date=29 April 2014 |access-date=29 April 2014}}</ref>
[[Robert Jenrick]] was elected in the subsequent by-election, in the Conservative Party's largest by-election majority for four decades. He was appointed on 24 July 2019 as Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government under Prime Minister Boris Johnson.
==Constituency profile== Many towns are historic in architecture<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/constituency/1150/newark | location=London | work=The Guardian | title=Newark Conservative: Patrick Mercer}}</ref> with many well-preserved [[listed building]]s<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://list.english-heritage.org.uk/mapsearch.aspx|title=Ordnance Survey map, courtesy of English Heritage|access-date=15 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120424060625/http://list.english-heritage.org.uk/mapsearch.aspx|archive-date=24 April 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> whereas much of the [[council housing]] in the constituency has been privately acquired under the [[right to buy]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/help/localstatistics|title=Local statistics - Office for National Statistics|website=www.ons.gov.uk}}</ref> Nonetheless, there is a minority of [[social housing]] but the proportion is lower than the national average across the three districts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129132219/http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html|url-status=dead|title=2011 census interactive maps|archive-date=29 January 2016}}</ref>
Labour held the seat for one term following their 1997 landslide victory, but subsequent major boundary changes have brought in more rural areas and made the seat into one of the most strongly Conservative voting in the UK.

|towns = [[Worksop]] and [[Retford]] |elects_howmany = One }} '''Bassetlaw''' {{IPAc-en|ˈ|b|æ|s|ᵻ|t|ˌ|l|ɔː}} is a [[United Kingdom constituencies|parliamentary constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} in [[Nottinghamshire]], represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019 general election]] by [[Brendan Clarke-Smith]], a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} Before that election, the seat had been part of the so-called "[[Red wall (British politics)|red wall]]", being held by the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] since [[1935 United Kingdom general election|1935]].
==Constituency profile== The Bassetlaw constituency is mostly rural and covers the north of [[Nottinghamshire]], including the towns of [[Worksop]] and [[Retford]]. It shares the name with the [[Bassetlaw District|Bassetlaw district]]. Parts of the constituency are former [[coal mining]] areas.
Residents' health and wealth are slightly below the UK average.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/seatdetails.py?seat=Bassetlaw|title = Seat Details - Bassetlaw}}</ref>
==Boundaries==
=== Historic === '''2010-2024''': Following its review of parliamentary boundaries in [[Nottinghamshire]], the [[Boundary Commission for England]] made changes to the constituency for the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]] to allow for population changes, most noticeably by returning the town of Retford from Newark, offset by moving the small town of [[Warsop|Market Warsop]] into Mansfield constituency.
The constituency included 22 electoral wards from Bassetlaw District Council: *[[Beckingham (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Beckingham]], [[Blyth (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Blyth]], [[Carlton (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Carlton]], [[Clayworth (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Clayworth]], [[East Retford East (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|East Retford East]], [[East Retford North (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|East Retford North]], [[East Retford South (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|East Retford South]], [[East Retford West (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|East Retford West]], [[Everton (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Everton]], [[Harworth (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Harworth]], [[Langold (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Langold]], [[Misterton (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Misterton]], [[Ranskill (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Ranskill]], [[Sturton (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Sturton]], [[Sutton (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Sutton]], [[Welbeck (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Welbeck]], [[Worksop East (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Worksop East]], [[Worksop North (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Worksop North]], [[Worksop North East (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Worksop North East]], [[Worksop North West (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Worksop North West]], [[Worksop South (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Worksop South]], [[Worksop South East (Bassetlaw electoral ward)|Worksop South East]].

==History== The constituency was created in 1885 by the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885|Redistribution of Seats Act]].
In March 2024, Cameron Holt was elected as the Member of [[UK Youth Parliament]] for Bassetlaw.<ref>https://www.worksopguardian.co.uk/news/politics/victory-for-bassetlaw-youth-mp-who-has-big-plans-for-the-future-4569756</ref><ref>https://www.bassetlaw.gov.uk/community-and-living/bassetlaw-youth-council/member-of-youth-parliament-cameron-holt/</ref>
===History of boundaries=== {{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Bassetlaw (UK Parliament constituency) 2010}}|frame=yes|frame-width=260|frame-height=210|text=Map of boundaries 2010-2024}} The Bassetlaw Division (named after one of the ancient [[Wapentakes]] of the county) as originally created in 1885 consisted of the municipal borough of [[East Retford]], the [[petty sessional division]]s of [[Retford]] and [[Worksop]] and part of [[Mansfield]] petty sessional division.
In 1918, the number of parliamentary divisions in [[Nottinghamshire]] was increased from four to five, with resulting changes in boundaries. Bassetlaw Division was now defined as containing the Municipal Borough of [[East Retford]], the [[Urban district (Great Britain and Ireland)|Urban District]]s of Warsop and Worksop, and the [[Rural District]]s of [[Blyth & Cuckney]], [[Misterton, Nottinghamshire|Misterton]] and East Retford, with the [[civil parish]] of [[Sookholme]] from [[Skegby]] Rural District.
In 1950, the five Parliamentary Divisions of Nottinghamshire were reorganised as six County Constituencies. Local government boundary changes in the 1930s now meant that Bassetlaw County Constituency was defined as comprising the Municipal Boroughs of East Retford and Worksop, the Urban District of [[Warsop]] and the Rural Districts of East Retford and Worksop.
In 1955, the Urban District of Warsop was moved into the Mansfield constituency.
The constituency's boundaries then remained unchanged until 1983. In that year, the town of East Retford and the neighbouring areas were transferred to the redrawn [[Newark (UK Parliament constituency)|Newark]] constituency. Bassetlaw constituency then comprised Worksop and surrounding areas in the Bassetlaw district as well as the town of Warsop in the [[Mansfield (district)|Mansfield]] district (see list of wards during this period below). There were no boundary changes in 1997.
From 1983 to 2010, the constituency comprised the following Bassetlaw district wards: *Beckingham, Blyth, Carlton, Clayworth, Everton, Harworth East, Harworth West, Hodsock, Misterton, Rampton, Ranskill, Sturton, Sutton, Welbeck, Worksop East, Worksop North, Worksop North East, Worksop North West, Worksop South, Worksop South East along with two Mansfield district wards: *Birklands, Meden (both in the Warsop area). In 2010 the two Mansfield District wards were transferred to the Mansfield constituency and the town of Retford was regained from Newark.

===Electoral history=== [[File:BassetlawGraph.svg|thumb|right|350px|Election results for Bassetlaw ([[1892 United Kingdom general election|1892]] - [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019]])]] On a historical measure, this had been a very [[safe seat]] for the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] before 2019, with their own or related candidates having held it since the [[1929 United Kingdom general election|1929 general election]]. On a size-of-majority measure, it was a low to medium safe seat. Its first [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] [[Malcolm MacDonald]] was one of the few Labour MPs to join his father [[Ramsay MacDonald]]'s [[UK National Government|National Government]]. MacDonald held the seat as a [[National Labour Organisation|National Labour]] candidate in the [[1931 United Kingdom general election|1931 election]], but was defeated at the next election in 1935 by Labour's [[Frederick Bellenger]].
Bellenger held the seat until he died in 1968. A [[by-election]] followed. The seat was retained for the Labour Party by [[Joe Ashton]] with a slender 1.72% majority, the narrowest since the 1920s. He held the seat until retirement at the [[2001 United Kingdom general election|2001 general election]]. He was succeeded at that year's election by fellow Labour politician [[John Mann (British politician)|John Mann]], who retained the seat at the next four elections. In 2019, Mann resigned being having been appointed to head a government inquiry on tackling anti-Semitism and to take a seat in the [[House of Lords]].<ref name="Mannquits">{{cite news |title=Labour's John Mann quits as MP to join House of Lords |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-50206257 |access-date=28 October 2019 |work=BBC News |date=28 October 2019}}</ref> The Labour candidate initially chosen to replace Mann, [[Sally Gimson]], was deselected before the election by the party's [[National Executive Committee of the Labour Party|National Executive Committee]] over what were described as "very serious allegations".<ref name=deselected>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-nottinghamshire-50322652 |title=Sally Gimson: Bassetlaw Labour candidate deselected by NEC |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=6 November 2019 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208224838/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-nottinghamshire-50322652 |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020}}</ref> Gimson referred to the process as a "kangaroo court", and Mann called the decision a stitch-up;<ref name=deselected/> Gimson started legal action against the party, but dropped the case several days later.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-nottinghamshire-50355077 |title=Deselected Bassetlaw candidate Sally Gimson drops legal fight |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=9 November 2019 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208225257/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-nottinghamshire-50355077 |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020}}</ref> Keir Morrison, a councillor in the [[Ashfield District]], replaced Gimson as the Labour candidate.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.lincolnshirelive.co.uk/news/local-news/new-labour-mp-candidate-announced-3526943 |title=New Labour MP candidate announced after selection row |last=McAllister |first=Richard |date=13 November 2019 |work=[[Lincolnshire Echo]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208225543/https://www.lincolnshirelive.co.uk/news/local-news/new-labour-mp-candidate-announced-3526943 |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020}}</ref>
In the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|December 2019 general election]], the Conservatives won the seat with a [[Swing (politics)|swing]] from Labour of 18.4%, the largest recorded in the election.<ref name=":0">{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/2019/12/13/conservatives-take-bassetlaw-with-biggest-swing-night-end-labour/ |title=Conservatives take Bassetlaw with biggest swing of night - ending 90 years of Labour dominance |last=Wright |first=Mike |date=13 December 2019 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208225838/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/2019/12/13/conservatives-take-bassetlaw-with-biggest-swing-night-end-labour/ |url-status=live |archive-date=8 February 2020 |access-date=8 February 2020 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> The fall in Labour's vote, 24.9%, was the greatest of any seat in the election.<ref name="TimesGuide19">{{cite book |title=The Times Guide to the House of Commons 2019 |date=2020 |publisher=Times Books |location=Glasgow |isbn=978-0-00-839258-1 |page=55}}</ref>

{{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 1885 onwards}} {{Distinguish|Electoral district of Mansfield|Mansfeld (electoral district)}}
{{EngvarB|date=June 2016}} {{Use dmy dates|date=June 2016}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Mansfield |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Mansfield (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East Midlands - Mansfield constituency.svg|175px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Mansfield in the East Midlands |year = 1885 |abolished = |type = County |previous = [[North Nottinghamshire (UK Parliament constituency)|North Nottinghamshire]] |next = |electorate = 74,680 (2023)<ref>{{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-east-midlands/#lg_mansfield-cc-74680 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – East Midlands |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=2 July 2024 |df=dmy }}</ref> |mp = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |party = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |region = England |county = [[Nottinghamshire]] |european = East Midlands |towns = [[Mansfield]] |elects_howmany = One }} '''Mansfield''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} created in 1885 represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since 2017 by [[Ben Bradley (politician)|Ben Bradley]] of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], who gained the seat at the [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017 general election]], from the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one Member of Parliament (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} This is the first time the seat has been represented by a Conservative since its creation in 1885.
The seat, centred on [[Mansfield]] in [[Nottinghamshire]], in recent times has been considered a relatively [[marginal seat]].<ref>[https://www.ft.com/content/05924dd8-461d-11e7-8519-9f94ee97d996 Odds lengthen on former UK mining town turning blue] ''[[Financial Times]]'', 1 June 2017. Retrieved 24 February 2024</ref><ref>[https://www.lgcplus.com/politics/devolution-and-economic-growth/exclusive-marginal-seats-dominate-latest-towns-funding-03-10-2023/ Marginal seats dominate latest towns funding] ''[[Local Government Chronicle]]'', 3 October 2023. Retrieved 24 February 2024</ref>
The Mansfield council area voted with more than 70% to [[Results of the 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum#West Midlands|Leave the European Union]] in the [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum|2016 referendum]]. In 2019, the Conservatives received 63.9% of the vote in the formerly safe Labour constituency.
==Boundaries==
=== Historic === '''1885–1918''': The sessional division of [[Mansfield]] (except the parishes of Clipstone, Sookholme and Warsop), and the parishes of Annesley, Eastwood, Felley and Greasley in the sessional division of [[Nottingham]].<ref>{{cite book |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=The Public General Acts of the United Kingdom passed in the forty-eighth and forty-ninth years of the reign of Queen Victoria |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/publicgeneralac01walegoog/page/n113/mode/2up |location=London |publisher=Eyre and Spottiswoode |pages=111–198 |date=1885 |chapter=Chap. 23. Redistribution of Seats Act, 1885 }}</ref>
'''1918–1950''': The municipal borough of [[Mansfield]], the urban district of Huthwaite, [[Mansfield Woodhouse Urban District|Mansfield Woodhouse]], and [[Sutton in Ashfield Urban District|Sutton-in-Ashfield]], and the rural district of [[Skegby Rural District|Skegby]] (except the parish of Sookholme).<ref>{{cite book |last=Fraser |first=Hugh |author-link=Hugh Fraser (British judge) |date=1918 |title=The Representation of the People Act, 1918: with explanatory notes |url=https://archive.org/details/representationof00frasrich |location=London |publisher=Sweet and Maxwell}}</ref>
'''1950–1955''': The municipal borough of Mansfield and the urban district of Sutton in Ashfield.<ref>{{Cite legislation UK |type=act |year=1948 |chapter=65 |act=Representation of the People Act 1948 |schedule=1 |accessdate=23 July 2023 }}</ref>
'''1955–1983''': The municipal borough of Mansfield and the urban districts of Mansfield Woodhouse and [[Warsop Urban District|Warsop]].<ref>{{cite book |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=1956 |title=Statutory Instruments 1955 |series=Part II |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8TDyAAAAMAAJ |chapter=The Parliamentary Constituencies (Nottinghamshire) Order 1955. SI 1955/169 |location=London |publisher=[[Her Majesty's Stationery Office]] |pages=2157–2159 |isbn=}}</ref>
'''1983–2010''': The Berry Hill, Broomhill, Cumberlands, Eakring, Forest Town, Ladybrook, Leeming, Lindhurst, Manor, Northfield, Oakham, Oak Tree, Pleasleyhill, Ravensdale, Sherwood and Titchfield wards of the [[Mansfield District|District of Mansfield]].<ref>{{cite legislation UK|type=si|si=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1983|year=1983|number=417|accessdate=23 July 2023}}</ref>
'''2010–2024''': The District of Mansfield.<ref>{{cite legislation UK|type=si|si=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007|year=2007|number=1681|accessdate=23 July 2023}}</ref>
The [[Boundary Commission for England]] made changes to the constituency to allow for regional and local population changes by moving the small town of [[Warsop|Market Warsop]] from [[Bassetlaw (UK Parliament constituency)|Bassetlaw]]. The boundaries since the [[Fifth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]] (coming into effect for the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]]) were coterminous with the [[Mansfield Borough Council|Borough of Mansfield]]. === Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the size of the constituency was reduced slightly to bring the electorate within the permitted electoral range by transferring the Bull Farm and Pleasley Hill ward and polling district BHC in the Berry Hill ward (as they existed on 1 December 2020) to [[Ashfield (UK Parliament constituency)|Ashfield]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part I}}</ref>
Following a local government boundary review in which came into effect in May 2023,<ref>{{Cite web |last=LGBCE |title=Mansfield {{!}} LGBCE |url=https://www.lgbce.org.uk/all-reviews/mansfield |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.lgbce.org.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Mansfield (Electoral Changes) Order 2022 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2022/777/contents/made}}</ref> the constituency now comprises the following wards of the Borough of Mansfield from the 2024 general election:
* Bancroft; Berry Hill; Brick Kiln; Carr Bank; Central; Eakring; Grange Farm; Holly Forest Town; Hornby; Kings Walk; Kingsway Forest Town; Lindhurst (part); Ling Forest; Manor; Market Warsop; Maun Valley Forest Town; Meden; Mill Lane; Netherfield; Newlands Forest Town; Oak Tree; Oakham; Park Hall; Penniment; Racecourse; Rock Hill; Rufford (majority); Sherwood (nearly all); Southwell; Thompsons; Vale; Wainwright; Warsop Carrs; West Bank; Yeoman Hill; and a very small part of Pleasley.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Seat Details - Mansfield |url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/calcwork23.py?seat=Mansfield |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.electoralcalculus.co.uk}}</ref>
The constituency covers the towns of [[Mansfield]] and [[Warsop]], Nottinghamshire.
==History== The seat was created in the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]] and in the mid-19th century to the mid-20th century its economy centred on coal mining and the market town itself. Among many classes of local labourers saw organised [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] support, in [[Trade Union]]s, party clubs and civic society. Progression in the party's polling was heightened from the early 1920s when the seat joined many wrested from the Liberal Party, enabling the formation of the [[First MacDonald ministry|first Labour government]]. By length of tenure and in great majorities a [[safe seat]] status emerged for Labour (on the basis of these standard criteria) in the 1950s and 1960s. In the 1980s general elections Labour's Mansfield candidates came closer to losing to [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]]s. At the [[1983 United Kingdom general election|1983 election]], Labour held the seat by just over 2,000 votes – at the following, in [[1987 United Kingdom general election|1987]], 56 votes. That election was set against the background of the party HQ-backed [[UK miners' strike (1984–1985)|miners' strike]] of 1984, not supported by the majority of miners in Nottinghamshire.
In the elections after 1987 until 2017, the Labour MP [[Alan Meale]] held Mansfield with relatively large majorities. He was [[Order of the British Empire|knighted]] in 2012 after receiving the award in the Queen's Birthday Honours list.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.chad.co.uk/news/local/mansfield-mp-sir-alan-meale-officially-knighted-by-prince-charles-1-4148520|title=Mansfield MP Sir Alan Meale officially knighted by Prince Charles|date=19 January 2012|work=Chad|access-date=11 May 2013|archive-date=21 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131221084238/http://www.chad.co.uk/news/local/mansfield-mp-sir-alan-meale-officially-knighted-by-prince-charles-1-4148520|url-status=dead}}</ref>
At the [[2005 United Kingdom general election|2005 general election]], [[Independent (politician)|independent]] candidate Stewart Rickersey, a local District Councillor, took 17% of the vote, finishing in third place.
At the 2010 general election, Andre Camilleri, another candidate from Mansfield Independent Forum and previously a local councillor with special responsibility as a Cabinet Member for Mansfield District Council during 2003 to 2007, was placed fourth with 9% of the vote, above the 5% deposit threshold.
At the 2015 general election, the [[UKIP]] candidate Sid Pepper received 25% of the vote placing him third; this dropped to 5% at the 2017 election.
At the 2019 general election, Ben Bradley held Mansfield with a 16,306 majority, the highest ever for a Conservative candidate.

[[Nottingham West (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham West]],
[[Rushcliffe (UK Parliament constituency)|Rushcliffe]] |elects_howmany2 = One }} '''Nottingham South''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]] of the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|Parliament of the United Kingdom]], represented since [[United Kingdom general election 2010|2010]] by [[Lilian Greenwood]] of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]].{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} {{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one Member of Parliament (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} ==Members of Parliament == Since 2010, the seat has been represented by [[Lilian Greenwood]], who succeeded Labour's Alan Simpson on his retirement. Simpson had held the seat since 1992, when he unseated the Conservative [[Martin Brandon-Bravo]]. === MPs 1885–1974 === ''[[Nottingham (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham]] prior to 1885'' {| [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] |} ==Constituency profile== The seat is the most economically diverse of the three Nottingham constituencies covering higher income and lower income output areas (sub-divisions of wards). In 2010 it was the most [[marginal seat|marginal of the seats]], changing hands on several occasions over the previous few decades, though is now a very safe Labour seat. There are below-national levels of unemployment claimants, for example at the end of 2010 male claimants were less than half as many as in [[Nottingham North (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham North]].{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2010/nov/17/unemployment-and-employment-statistics-economics |title=Unemployment: the key UK data and benefit claimants for every constituency |date=15 May 2013 |author=Simon Rogers, John Burn-Murdoch and Ami Sedghi |work=The Guardian |access-date=28 December 2014 }} The Labour majority has since grown to 6,000 in 2015 and over 15,000 in 2017, making it a safe seat. The constituency is also the most politically diverse of the three city seats which together form [[Nottingham City Council]]. In the 2007 elections for Nottingham City Council, the constituency elected 9 of the 42 Labour councillors, 6 of the 7 Conservatives and 5 of the 6 Liberal Democrats.{{cite web|url=http://www.nottinghamcity.gov.uk/index.aspx?articleid=940 |title=Local Election Results May 2007 |publisher=Nottingham City Council |access-date=28 December 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615193232/http://www.nottinghamcity.gov.uk/index.aspx?articleid=940 |archive-date=15 June 2011 }} ==Boundaries == === Historic === '''1885–1918''': The Municipal Borough of Nottingham wards of Bridge, Castle, Market, Meadow, St Mary, and Trent. '''1918–1955''': The County Borough of Nottingham wards of Bridge, Castle, Meadows, and Trent. '''1955–1974''': The County Borough of Nottingham wards of Bridge, Clifton, Lenton, and Trent, and the Urban District of West Bridgford. '''1983–2010''': The City of Nottingham wards of Abbey, Bridge, Clifton East, Clifton West, Lenton, Park, Robin Hood, Wilford, and Wollaton. '''2010–2024''': The City of Nottingham wards of Bridge, Clifton North, Clifton South, Dunkirk and Lenton, Leen Valley, Radford and Park, Wollaton East and Lenton Abbey, and Wollaton West. === Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 December 2020): * The City of Nottingham wards of Bilborough, Clifton East, Clifton West, Lenton & Wollaton East, Meadows, Radford, and Wollaton West.{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule 1 Part 1 East Midlands}} ''Nottingham city centre was transferred to [[Nottingham East (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham East]] and Leen Valley to the newly created seat of [[Nottingham North and Kimberley (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham North and Kimberley]], with the Bilborough ward being transferred from the abolished [[Nottingham North (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham North]] constituency.'' Nottingham South contains at least parts of both of the city's universities. The [[University of Nottingham]]'s [[Campuses of the University of Nottingham|University Park Campus and Jubilee Campus]] are both in the constituency, as is the [[Nottingham Trent University|Clifton Campus of Nottingham Trent University]]. Many of these students are based in rows of terraced housing in the Lenton and Radford wards of this seat. A minority of students and much of the universities' staff are based in neighbouring Beeston, but this falls within the [[Broxtowe (UK Parliament constituency)|Broxtowe]] constituency. ==History== Since as [[Model Parliament|early as 1295]], Nottingham was represented by [[Nottingham (UK Parliament constituency)|one large constituency]] which elected two members of parliament to the House of Commons. Under a [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885|major Act of 1885]] three single-member subdivisions were created: [[Nottingham East]], [[Nottingham West (UK Parliament constituency)|Nottingham West]] and Nottingham South. ;Nine year absence of the seat Nottingham South was abolished in the election of February 1974 but was re-formed with altered boundaries nine years later in 1983 from parts of Nottingham East and Nottingham West. ;Modern demography Nottingham South is the most diverse of the three constituencies in terms of economic demographics. It includes areas of higher incomes than average in the form of [[Wollaton]] and [[The Park Estate]]{{cite web |url=http://neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk |title=2001 Census |publisher=The Office for National Statistics |access-date=28 December 2014 }} and areas of relative poverty, both suburban and inner city. The [[council estate]] built next to and within the bounds of the village/[[ecclesiastical parish|parish]] of [[Clifton, Nottingham|Clifton]] was once the largest in Europe. Results to date excluding under the [[Premiership of Tony Blair|Blair Ministry]] when it was quite firmly Labour have produced the most marginal majorities of Nottingham City's three constituencies. The [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] [[Martin Brandon-Bravo]] held the seat from 1983 to 1992. Since 1992, Nottingham South has been held by [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] MPs; [[Alan Simpson (Member of Parliament)|Alan Simpson]] until retiring from the House of Commons in 2010 and [[Lilian Greenwood]] from 2010. [[File:Wollaton Hall small.jpg|thumb|left|300px|Wollaton Hall in Wollaton, one of the constituency's more affluent areas.]] Communities or localities in Nottingham South include: * [[Clifton, Nottingham|Clifton]] * [[Dunkirk, Nottingham|Dunkirk]] * [[Hockley Village]] * [[Lace Market]] * [[Leen Valley]] * [[Lenton Abbey]] * [[Lenton, Nottingham|Lenton]] * Parts of [[Nottingham City Centre]] * [[Radford, Nottingham|Radford]] * [[The Meadows, Nottingham|The Meadows]] * [[The Park Estate]] * [[Wollaton]] ==Elections == [[File:NottinghamSouthGraph.svg|thumb|right|350px|Election results for Nottingham South]] === Elections in the 2020s === {{Election box begin|title=[[2024 United Kingdom general election|General election 2024]]: Nottingham South[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election/2024/uk/constituencies/E14001412 Nottingham South] }} {{Election box candidate with party link|party=Independent politician|candidate=Shaghofta Akhtar|votes=|percentage=|change=|}} {{Election box candidate with party link |party = Workers Party of Britain |candidate = Paras Ghazni{{Cite web|url=https://workerspartybritain.org/general-election-2024/|title=General Election candidates |access-date=4 June 2024 |publisher=[[Workers Party of Britain]]}} |votes = |percentage = |change = }} {{Election box candidate with party link|party=Labour Party (UK)|candidate=[[Lilian Greenwood]]{{cite tweet|user=LilianGreenwood|author=[[Lilian Greenwood]]|number= 1498243673238159361 |date=28 February 2022|title=Proud and delighted to have been unanimously backed by #NottinghamSouth @UKLabour branches, affiliated trade unions and socialist societies to be our candidate at the next General Election. |party = [[Reform UK]] |region = England |county = [[Nottinghamshire]] |european = East Midlands |elects_howmany = One }} '''Ashfield''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[UK Parliament]]. It is in the English county of [[Nottinghamshire]], [[East Midlands]], to the north west of the city of [[Nottingham]] in the [[River Erewash|Erewash]] Valley along the border with neighbouring county [[Derbyshire]].
Ashfield was part of the [[Red wall (British politics)|Red Wall]], a group of constituencies in the [[Midlands]] and [[Northern England]] which formerly almost always voted for the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]], until many of them switched to the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] in the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019 general election]]. In the [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum|2016 referendum on membership of the European Union]], Ashfield voted 70% in favour of [[Brexit]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.itv.com/news/calendar/update/2016-06-24/eu-referendum-ashfield-votes-to-leave-the-eu/|title=EU Referendum: Ashfield votes to LEAVE the EU|website=ITV News|language=en|access-date=18 March 2020}}</ref>
== Constituency profile == The seat contains the [[market town]]s of [[Kirkby-in-Ashfield]], [[Sutton-in-Ashfield]] and [[Huthwaite]]. Coal mining was formerly a significant part of the local economy. [[Electoral Calculus]] categorises the seat as having socially conservative views and economically soft left views alongside strong support for [[Brexit]]. Around 57% of the constituency is [[multiple deprivation index|deprived]], slightly higher than the national average of 52%, according to the site. The average age is 50.8, at least 80% of the local population owns a car, whilst 68% own a home, and the gross household income is £35,124.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Electoral Calculus’ profile of Ashfield|url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/calcwork23.py?seat=Ashfield |website=Electoral Calculus |access-date=14 June 2024}}</ref>
== Boundaries ==
=== Historic === {{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Ashfield (UK Parliament constituency) 2010}}|frame=yes|frame-width=200|text=Map of boundaries 2010–2024}} '''1955–1974''': The Urban Districts of Eastwood, Kirkby-in-Ashfield, and Sutton-in-Ashfield, and in the Rural District of Basford the parishes of Annesley, Bestwood Park, Brinsley, Felley, Linby, Newstead, Papplewick, and Selston.
'''1974–1983''': The Urban Districts of Hucknall, Kirkby-in-Ashfield, and Sutton-in-Ashfield, and in the Rural District of Basford the parishes of Annesley, Felley, and Selston.
'''1983–2010''': The District of Ashfield wards of Jacksdale, Kirkby-in-Ashfield Central, Kirkby-in-Ashfield East, Kirkby-in-Ashfield West, Selston, Sutton-in-Ashfield Central, Sutton-in-Ashfield East, Sutton-in-Ashfield North, Sutton-in-Ashfield West, Underwood, and Woodhouse, and the Borough of Broxtowe wards of Brinsley, Eastwood East, Eastwood North, and Eastwood South.
'''2010–2024''': The District of Ashfield wards of Jacksdale, Kirkby-in-Ashfield Central, Kirkby-in-Ashfield East, Kirkby-in-Ashfield West, Selston, Sutton-in-Ashfield Central, Sutton-in-Ashfield East, Sutton-in-Ashfield North, Sutton-in-Ashfield West, Underwood, and Woodhouse, and the Borough of Broxtowe wards of Brinsley, Eastwood North and Greasley Beauvale, and Eastwood South.
=== Current === Following the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], and reflecting the local government boundary review in the District of Mansfield which came into effect in May 2023,<ref>{{Cite web |last=LGBCE |title=Mansfield {{!}} LGBCE |url=https://www.lgbce.org.uk/all-reviews/mansfield |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.lgbce.org.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Mansfield (Electoral Changes) Order 2022 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2022/777/contents/made}}</ref> the constituency is composed of the following with effect from the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]]:
* The District of Ashfield wards of: Abbey Hill; Annesley & Kirkby Woodhouse; Ashfields; Carsic; Central & New Cross; Huthwaite & Brierley; Jacksdale; Kingsway; Kirkby Cross & Portland; Larwood; Leamington; St. Mary’s; Selston; Skegby; Stanton Hill & Teversal; Summit; Sutton Junction & Harlow Wood; The Dales; Underwood.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part I}}</ref>
* Parts of the District of Mansfield wards of: Lindhurst; Pleaseley; Rufford; Sherwood.<sup>1</sup> <ref>{{Cite web |title=New Seat Details – Ashfield |url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/calcwork23.py?seat=Ashfield |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.electoralcalculus.co.uk}}</ref> ''The parts in the Borough of Broxtowe were transferred to the [[Broxtowe (UK Parliament constituency)|Broxtowe]] constituency and the parts in Mansfield District were transferred from the [[Mansfield (UK Parliament constituency)|Mansfield]] constituency.''
== History == Until the Conservatives gained the seat at the 2019 general election, it was almost always a [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] seat since its creation for the [[1955 United Kingdom general election|1955 general election]]. The Ashfield constituency has been served by a former Secretary of State, [[Geoff Hoon]], and since its creation until 2019, for only two years has been served by one member of another party, [[Tim Smith (UK politician)|Tim Smith]] of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], from [[1977 Ashfield by-election|1977]] to [[1979 United Kingdom general election|1979]]. Ashfield's 2019 result indicates [[safe seat|quite a large Conservative majority]]. In 2010, the seat had a [[marginal seat|marginal majority]] of only 192 votes over the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]], but this was increased to 8,820 in 2015 after a collapse in the Liberal Democrat vote, with the Conservatives finishing in second place. In 2017, there was another narrow margin of victory for Labour after an 8.9% swing to the Conservatives, who squeezed most of the fairly substantial [[UKIP]] vote from two years earlier, and also a large vote for the [[Ashfield Independents]] candidate of nearly 10%, but Labour on that occasion did just enough to hang on by just over 400 votes. In 2019, the Ashfield Independents candidate [[Jason Zadrozny]], who had come close to winning the seat for the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]] nine years earlier, came second with a substantial vote, and the Conservatives took the seat despite achieving fewer votes and a smaller percentage of the total vote than in 2017.

{{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 1885 onwards}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Rushcliffe |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Rushcliffe (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East Midlands - Rushcliffe constituency.svg|175px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Rushcliffe in the East Midlands |map_entity = [[Nottinghamshire]] |map_year =2024 |year = 1885 |abolished = |type = County |previous = [[South Nottinghamshire (UK Parliament constituency)|South Nottinghamshire]] |next = |electorate = 79,160 (2024)<ref>{{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-east-midlands/#lg_rushcliffe-cc-76171 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – East Midlands |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=3 July 2024 |df=dmy }}</ref> |mp = [[James Naish|James Naish]] |party = [[Labour_Party_(UK)|Labour]] |region = England |county = [[Nottinghamshire]] |towns = [[West Bridgford]], [[Cotgrave]], [[Radcliffe-on-Trent]], [[Keyworth]], [[East Leake]] |elects_howmany = One }}
'''Rushcliffe''' is a [[Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} in [[Nottinghamshire]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] from [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024]] by [[James Naish]], a [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour MP]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}}
From 1970 until 2019, it was represented by [[Kenneth Clarke]] who was [[Father of the House (United Kingdom)|Father of the House of Commons]] for his last two years as an MP. He was appointed to the executive in the governments of [[Margaret Thatcher]], [[John Major]] and [[David Cameron]] – one of five ministers to serve the whole 18 years of the Thatcher and Major governments. His political career is the fifth-longest in the modern era;{{clarify|date=April 2021}} he remains a notable figure in British politics.
==History== The constituency was formed by the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]] (for first use during the election that year).
Between 1950 and 2019, it was considered to have been a [[safe seat]] for the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], whose members have held it without [[marginal seat|marginal majorities]], except for a four-year period from 1966 when it was held by [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]], coinciding with the [[Labour government, 1964–1970|first Wilson ministry]]. Unlike other constituencies nearby, such as [[Broxtowe (UK Parliament constituency)|Broxtowe]] and [[Gedling (UK Parliament constituency)|Gedling]], which were previously held by the Conservatives, they retained Rushcliffe in the [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997 New Labour landslide]] but it was won by Labour in the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 Labour landslide]]
In the [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum|2016 European Union membership referendum]], it was the only constituency in the Nottinghamshire and overall [[East Midlands]] region to vote Remain (57.6% to 42.4%), even as neighbouring city of [[Nottingham]] voted to Leave (50.8% to 49.2%).<ref>{{Cite web |title=EU Referendum Results - BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/politics/eu_referendum/results |access-date=2022-12-20 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref> This can be attributed to the constituency's affluence, as well as then-MP Kenneth Clarke's pro-EU political leanings (he would be the only Conservative MP to vote against triggering [[United Kingdom invocation of Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union|Article 50]] in 2017.)<ref>{{Cite web |last=Harper |first=Christopher |date=2019-09-04 |title=Brexit: How did Rushcliffe vote during the 2016 EU referendum? |url=https://www.nottinghampost.com/news/uk-world-news/brexit-rushcliffe-mp-ken-clarke-3282777 |access-date=2022-12-20 |website=NottinghamshireLive |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Locker |first=Joseph |date=2019-09-08 |title=Ken Clarke on 'ruthless' Boris, Brexit and his supportive constituents |url=https://www.nottinghampost.com/news/local-news/ken-clarke-rushcliffe-brexit-country-3297278 |access-date=2022-12-20 |website=NottinghamshireLive |language=en}}</ref>

=== Historic === '''1885–1918''': Part of the Sessional Division of Nottingham.
'''1918–1950''': The Urban Districts of Beeston, Carlton, and West Bridgford, the Rural Districts of Leake and Stapleford, the Rural District which consisted of the parishes of Kingston-on-Soar and Ratcliffe-on-Soar, and in the Rural District of Basford the parishes of Awsworth, Barton-in-Fabis, Bilborough, Bradmore, Bunny, Burton Joyce, Clifton-with-Glapton, Colwick, Cossall, Gamston, Gedling, Gotham, Nuthall, Ruddington, South Wilford, Stoke Bardolph, Strelley, Thrumpton, Trowell, and Wollaton.
'''1950–1955''': The Urban Districts of Beeston and Stapleford, and West Bridgford, and in the Rural District of Basford the parishes of Barton-in-Fabis, Bilborough, Bradmore, Bunny, Clifton with Glapton, Colwick, Costock, East Leake, Gedling, Gotham, Kingston-on-Soar, Normanton-on-Soar, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, Rempstone, Ruddington, Stanford-on-Soar, Sutton Bonington, Thorpe-in-the-Glebe, Thrumpton, West Leake, Willoughby-on-the-Wolds, and Wysall.
'''1955–1974''': The Urban District of Beeston and Stapleford, and in the Rural District of Basford the parishes of Barton-in-Fabis, Bilborough, Bradmore, Bunny, Colwick, Costock, East Leake, Gedling, Gotham, Kingston-on-Soar, Normanton-on-Soar, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, Rempstone, Ruddington, Stanford-on-Soar, Sutton Bonington, Thorpe-in-the-Glebe, Thrumpton, West Leake, Willoughby-on-the-Wolds, and Wysall.
'''1974–1983''': The Urban District of West Bridgford, the Rural District of Bingham, and in the Rural District of Basford the parishes of Barton-in-Fabis, Bradmore, Bunny, Costock, East Leake, Gotham, Kingston on Soar, Normanton on Soar, Ratcliffe on Soar, Rempstone, Ruddington, Stanford on Soar, Sutton Bonington, Thorpe in the Glebe, Thrumpton, West Leake, Willoughby-on-the-Wolds, and Wysall.
'''1983–2010''': The [[Rushcliffe|Borough of Rushcliffe]].
'''2010–2024''': The Borough of Rushcliffe wards of Abbey, Bunny, Compton Acres, Cotgrave, Cropwell, Edwalton, Gamston, Gotham, Keyworth and the Wolds, Lady Bay, Leake, Lutterell, Musters,Nevile and Langar, Newton, Radcliffe-on-Trent, Ruddington, Soar Valley, Tollerton, and Trent Bridge.<ref>https://www.rushcliffe.gov.uk/elections/ward-boundaries-and-maps/</ref>
=== Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency was defined as follows (as they existed on 1 December 2020):
* The Borough of Rushcliffe wards of: Abbey; Bunny; Compton Acres; Cotgrave; Cropwell; Edwalton; Gamston North; Gamston South; Gotham; Keyworth & Wolds; Lady Bay; Leake; Lutterell; Musters; Nevile & Langar; Radcliffe on Trent; Ruddington; Sutton Bonington; Tollerton; Trent Bridge.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule 1 Part 1 East Midlands}}</ref>
''The constituency saw minor boundary changes due to the redrawing of local authority ward boundaries.''
Following a further local government boundary review in which came into effect in May 2023,<ref>{{Cite web |last=LGBCE |title=Rushcliffe {{!}} LGBCE |url=https://www.lgbce.org.uk/all-reviews/rushcliffe |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.lgbce.org.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Rushcliffe (Electoral Changes) Order 2022 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2022/1364/contents/made}}</ref> the constituency now comprises the following wards of the Borough of Rushcliffe from the 2024 general election:
* Abbey; Bunny; Compton Acres; Cotgrave; Cropwell; Edwalton; Gamston; Gotham; Keyworth & Wolds; Lady Bay; Leake; Lutterell; Musters; Nevile & Langar (nearly all); Newton (part); Radcliffe on Trent; Ruddington; Soar Valley; Tollerton; Trent Bridge.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Seat Details - Rushcliffe |url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/calcwork23.py?seat=Rushcliffe |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=www.electoralcalculus.co.uk}}</ref>
==Constituency profile== The main town in the constituency is [[West Bridgford]], which is part of the [[Greater Nottingham]] urban area, and includes the [[Trent Bridge]] [[cricket]] ground and [[Nottingham Forest F.C.]], and has some strong Labour wards like Trent Bridge itself, Lady Bay and the village of Ruddington. The remainder of the constituency is predominantly rural and Conservative, including the villages of [[Cotgrave]], [[East Leake]], [[Sutton Bonington]], [[Keyworth]] and [[Radcliffe on Trent]].
The constituency consists of Census Output Areas of one local government district with a working population whose income is close to the national average and has lower than average reliance upon [[social housing]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk|title=Local statistics - Office for National Statistics|website=neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk}}</ref> At the end of 2012 the unemployment rate in the constituency stood as 1.9% of the population claiming jobseekers allowance, compared to the regional average of 3.5%.<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2010/nov/17/unemployment-and-employment-statistics-economics Unemployment claimants by constituency] ''[[The Guardian]]''</ref> The borough contributing to the bulk of the seat has a low 15.1% of its population without a car, 16.4% of the population without qualifications and a very high 39.0% with level 4 qualifications or above. In terms of tenure a high 76.7% of homes are owned outright or on a mortgage as at the 2011 census across the district.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html|title=2011 census interactive maps|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129132219/http://www.ons.gov.uk/ons/guide-method/census/2011/census-data/2011-census-interactive-content/index.html|archive-date=2016-01-29}}</ref>
